C. Naloxone
Explanation
Naloxone: Opioid antagonist that rapidly reverses respiratory depression caused by opioid overdose. Given intravenously (IV), intramuscularly (IM), subcutaneously (SC), or intranasally. Short duration of action, requiring repeated doses or infusion

Other options:
A) Methadone: Used for opioid dependence treatment (maintenance therapy in opioid addiction)
B) Flumazenil: Antidote for benzodiazepine overdose, not opioids. Used in cases of sedation or respiratory depression due to benzodiazepine
D) Oximes: Used for organophosphate poisoning (cholinesterase inhibitors). Not effective in opioid poisoning

q: A girl has been brought to emergency with paracetamol poisoning. The antidote is?
e:
C. N acetyl cysteine
Explanation
N-acetylcysteine (NAC) replenishes glutathione, which detoxifies NAPQI, the toxic metabolite of paracetamol, preventing liver damage

Other options:
A) Atropine used as an antidote for organophosphate poisoning and bradycardia, not paracetamol toxicity
B) Flumazenil: Benzodiazepine antagonist, used to reverse benzodiazepine overdose
D) Naloxone: An opioid antagonist, used to treat opioid overdose (e.g., morphine, heroin)

q: Identify the injury
e:
A. Incised looking lacerated wound
Explanation
Incised-looking lacerated wound caused by blunt trauma may have clean edges resembling an incised wound but show tissue bridging and irregular margins on close inspection

Other options:
B) Incised wound caused by a sharp object like a knife, with smooth, well-defined edges and no tissue bridging
C) Lacerated-looking wound: not a standard forensic term, possibly confusing with option A
D) Lacerated wound is caused by blunt trauma, they typically have irregular margins, not an incised appearance

q: While recording evidence in a court of law, the lawyer asked the witness- “did you see that Mr A killed Mr B?. This type of question is permitted in
e:
B. Cross examination
Explanation
Cross-Examination conducted by the opposing lawyer to challenge the witness’s testimony. Leading questions are permitted to test the credibility of the witness

Other options:
A) Examination-in-Chief: This is the initial questioning of a witness by the party who called them. Leading questions are not allowed, except in special circumstances
C) Re-Examination: Conducted by the original lawyer after cross-examination. Used to clarify doubts raised during cross-examination
D) Direct Examination: Another term for examination-in-chief. Leading questions are not allowed

q: Not suggestive of cocaine poisoning is
e:
A. Brady cardia
Explanation
Cocaine is a sympathomimetic drug that increases norepinephrine and dopamine levels. This leads to tachycardia, hypertension, and arrhythmias, not bradycardia

Other options:
B) Hyperthermia: Cocaine-induced vasoconstriction and increased muscle activity can cause severe hyperthermia, which is a life-threatening condition
C) Agitation: Cocaine stimulates the CNS, leading to agitation, restlessness, paranoia, and hallucinations
D) Incoordination: Cocaine can cause neurological impairment, including tremors, incoordination, and seizures

q: Active principle of this seed is
e:
C. Bhilawanol
Explanation
Bhilawanol, active principle of Semecarpus anacardium (Marking Nut), which causes allergic dermatitis and blister formation

Other options:
A) Crotoninol not a recognized active compound in toxic seeds
B) Ricinol: Ricinus communis (Castor seed) contains ricin, not ricinol
D) Abrin: Active toxin in Abrus precatorius (Rosary Pea), causing severe poisoning by inhibiting protein synthesis

q: True regarding the change seen in this image is
e:
B. Dur to sulph hemoglobin
Explanation
Marbling occurs due to the reaction of hydrogen sulfide (H?S) produced by putrefactive bacteria with hemoglobin, forming sulfhemoglobin, which gives the veins a greenish-black discoloration

Other options:
A) Due to vascular diseases: Marbling is a postmortem change, not related to any vascular disease
C) Due to non-bacterial causes: bacterial decomposition plays a crucial role in marbling
D) Seen within 24 hours of death: Marbling typically appears 24–48 hours postmortem, progressing over time

q: This phenomenon is due to
o: Immersion in water for more than 36 hrs
e:
D. Immersion in water for more than 36 hrs
Explanation
Washerwoman’s feet (or hands) occur due to prolonged immersion in water, leading to skin wrinkling and maceration. This is commonly seen in drowned bodies or corpses left in water for extended periods

Other options:
A) Colliquative Putrefaction: This refers to the liquefaction of tissues due to decomposition. It is a late postmortem change but not specifically linked to washerwoman feet
B) Postmortem Hanging: Hanging causes pallor, ligature marks, and petechiae, but it does not lead to wrinkling of the skin like washerwoman’s feet
C) Torture in Hot Water: Burns and skin peeling (epidermolysis) occur in hot water torture, NOT the wrinkling seen in washerwoman’s feet

q: Wife gave birth to twins. The suspicious husband underwent DNA typing, where he found out that he was not the father of one of the twins. Such cases are known aas
e:
B. Superfecundaition
Explanation
Superfecundation happens when two different eggs are fertilized by sperm from different fathers during the same ovulatory cycle. This explains why the husband was the biological father of one twin but not the other

Other options:
A) Superfetation: This occurs when a second ovum is fertilized during an ongoing pregnancy, leading to twins with different gestational ages. Extremely rare in humans, more common in animals
C) Papyraceous Child: This refers to one twin dying in utero and being compressed against the uterine wall, leading to a thin, paper-like fetus
D) Suppositious Child: This refers to a child fraudulently claimed as another's, such as in inheritance disputes

q: A person used to sit naked on his balcony while drinking coffee, facing a crowded park. This paraphilia is called as
e:
B. Exhibitionism
Explanation
Exhibitionism is a paraphilic disorder characterized by the urge to expose one’s genitals or engage in indecent behavior in public, often for sexual gratification

Other options:
A) Voyeurism involves watching others (often in private settings) without their consent for sexual pleasure
C) Masochism refers to deriving pleasure from pain or humiliation inflicted on oneself
D) Fetishism involves sexual fixation on non-living objects or specific body parts (e.g., shoes, feet)

q: A laborer was working in the field in the afternoon of a hot summer and suddenly collapsed. Which of the following is not seen
e:
A. Sweating
Explanation
The laborer likely experienced heat stroke, a life-threatening condition caused by prolonged exposure to high temperatures and failure of thermoregulation Sweating is not seen in classic heat stroke because thermoregulation fails, leading to anhidrosis (absence of sweating). Sweating is more common in heat exhaustion, a milder condition

Other options:
B) Disorientation: Seen in heat stroke due to CNS dysfunction
C) Hot skin: Core body temperature rises above 40°C, leading to dry, hot skin due to thermoregulatory failure
D) Tachycardia: The body compensates with an increased heart rate to maintain circulation

q: A healthy child plucked a fruit while going to play. He consumed the fruit. After some time, he developed symptoms of irritability, restlessness, confusion, inability to pass urine, hot skin and photophobia. Select the poison and the antidote
e:
A. Dhatura and physostigmine
Explanation
The symptoms described irritability, restlessness, confusion, inability to pass urine, hot skin, and photophobia are classic anticholinergic symptoms, which strongly suggest Datura (Dhatura) poisoning. Datura contains tropane alkaloids like atropine, scopolamine, and hyoscyamine, leading to anticholinergic toxicity Dhatura poisoning causes anticholinergic toxicity (dry mouth, mydriasis, hallucinations, urinary retention, fever) Physostigmine, a cholinesterase inhibitor, reverses the effects by increasing acetylcholine levels. Other Options: B) Yellow Oleander and Physostigmine: Yellow oleander poisoning affect the heart by causing cardiac glycoside toxicity (arrhythmias, vomiting, hyperkalemia). Digibind (Digoxin-specific antibody fragments) is the antidote, not physostigmine C) Dhatura and Digibind: Digibind is used for cardiac glycoside poisoning, not anticholinergic toxicity D) Yellow Oleander and Digibind: This pair would be correct for yellow oleander poisoning but does not match the symptoms given in the question

q: A person abstained from alcohol for 3 days. He has brought to the hospital with disorientation, irritability, paranoid delusions, visual hallucinations and altered sensorium. The diagnosis is
e:
D. Delirium tremens
Explanation
The patient has a history of alcohol abstinence for 3 days, followed by disorientation, irritability, paranoid delusions, visual hallucinations, and altered sensorium. These symptoms strongly suggest severe alcohol withdrawal, specifically Delirium Tremens (DT) DT typically occurs 48–96 hours after alcohol cessation in chronic alcohol users Symptoms include confusion, hallucinations (often visual), autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension, fever), tremors, and agitation Management: Benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam, diazepam), fluids, thiamine, and supportive care

Other options:
A) Korsakoff Psychosis is a chronic complication of Wernicke encephalopathy due to thiamine deficiency. Features anterograde and retrograde amnesia, confabulation, but no acute disorientation, hallucinations, or altered sensorium seen in DT
B) Wernicke Encephalopathy caused by thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency in alcoholics. Classic triad: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion
C) Acute Alcoholic Hallucinosis occurs within 12–24 hours of alcohol withdrawal (earlier than DT). Patient remains alert and oriented (unlike the altered sensorium seen in DT). Hallucinations are usually auditory, whereas DT mainly has visual hallucinations

q: A person giving false evidence under oath will be punished under
e:
C. Section 193 IPC
Explanation
Section 193 IPC – Specifies punishment for giving false evidence under oath

Other options:
Section 191 IPC – Defines giving false evidence (perjury) Section 192 IPC – Defines fabricating false evidence (creating false evidence) Section 197 IPC – Deals with prosecution of public servants for official acts

q: In case of civil negligence during medical practice, the onus of proof lies on
e:
B. The patient
Explanation
In cases of civil negligence during medical practice, the burden of proof (onus of proof) lies on the patient. The patient must prove the following elements • Duty of care – The doctor had a duty to treat the patient • Breach of duty – The doctor failed to follow the standard of care • Causation – The breach directly caused harm to the patient • Damages – The patient suffered actual harm or injury due to the negligence Other Options: A) The doctor – In civil cases, the doctor is the defendant and is not required to prove innocence unless the court applies the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur (where negligence is so obvious that no further proof is needed) C) The hospital – The hospital may be vicariously liable for the doctor’s negligence, but the initial burden of proof is on the patient D) The lawyer – The lawyer represents the plaintiff or defendant but does not hold the burden of proof

q: Poison which can be detected even in exhumated decomposed bodies
e:
B. Arsenic
Explanation
Arsenic is a heavy metal that gets deposited in bones, hair, and nails, making it detectable even after decomposition

Other options:
Mercury, Copper, and Bismuth also persist in tissues, but arsenic is the most stable and reliably detected in exhumed bodies Toxicological analysis using atomic absorption spectroscopy or ICP-MS can identify arsenic in remains years after burial

q: Magnan’s symptom is seen in case of poisoning by
e:
B. Cocaine
Explanation
Magnan’s Symptom refers to the hallucination of insects crawling under the skin (formication) and is highly characteristic of cocaine poisoning. It is often associated with cocaine-induced psychosis, which includes paranoia, agitation, and tactile hallucinations

Other options:
A) Cannabis – Can cause paranoia and hallucinations but does not typically lead to formication
C) LSD – Causes visual and auditory hallucinations but not formication
D) Datura – Causes anticholinergic toxicity, delirium, and hallucinations, but not Magnan’s symptom

q: Invisible tattoos during autopsy can be detected by
e:
C. Regional lymph node biopsy
Explanation
Invisible tattoos refer to tattoo pigment particles that have migrated from the skin to regional lymph nodes over time. During an autopsy, if the tattoo is faded or removed, pigment deposits can still be detected in lymph nodes draining the tattooed region

Other options:
UV and infrared rays (Options A &
B) are used in forensic imaging for latent bruises or injuries, not tattoo detection Local skin biopsy (Option
D) would be helpful for microscopic analysis but does not address cases where tattoos have faded or been removed

q: In case of sexual assault to a child, the hymen may not be ruptured because:
e:
B. Hymen is deeply seated
Explanation
In cases of sexual assault in children, the hymen may remain intact due to its deeply seated position in prepubertal girls Other Options: A) Elasticity of hymen: While some hymens are elastic, the deep-seated position is the primary reason for non-rupture in children C) Hymen is underdeveloped: The hymen is present from birth; it is not considered "underdeveloped" but rather varies in thickness and shape D) Hymen is tough in structure: Hymenal toughness varies among individuals, but deep positioning is the main factor in children

q: Most widely used illegal drug is
e:
D. Cannabis
Explanation
Cannabis (marijuana) is the most widely used illegal drug globally According to the UNODC (United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime), cannabis has the highest prevalence of use among illicit substances

Other options:
Tobacco (Option
B) is widely consumed, it is not illegal in most countries Cocaine (Option
A) and amphetamines (Option
C) are also used but have significantly lower global usage compared to cannabis

q: According to the Mental Health Act, the maximum duration possible for voluntary admission is
e:
D. 30 days
Explanation
A voluntary patient can remain admitted for a maximum of 30 days, after which a review is required. If further hospitalization is needed, the mental health professional must assess and extend the admission accordingly

Other options:
A) 24 hours: This duration applies to emergency admissions under the act, not voluntary ones
B) 48 hours: This applies to assessment and review periods for involuntary admissions but not for voluntary patients
C) 15 days: While some emergency care admissions may last for shorter periods, voluntary admission can extend up to 30 days before reassessment

q: In case of rape, a sample was taken from the vagina and was stained with And yellow needle shaped crystals of picrate were detected. Which test is this?
e:
A. Barberio’s test
Explanation
Barberio test is a chemical test used to detect spermine in seminal stains. In this test, the sample is treated with picric acid or gold chloride, which results in the formation of yellow, needle-shaped crystals, confirming the presence of spermine. This test is often used in forensic investigations for semen detection in rape cases

Other options:
Florence test (Option B): Detects choline in seminal stains by forming brown rhombic crystals with iodine solution Ammonium molybdate test (Option C): Used for detecting phosphates, not spermine Acid phosphatase test (Option D): Detects acid phosphatase, an enzyme present in semen, but does not produce yellow needle-shaped crystals

q: The given image shows
e:
B. Decomposition
Explanation
Decomposition refers to the post-mortem breakdown of tissues due to bacterial and enzymatic activity. The early changes seen in decomposition include • Blisters (skin slippage) due to epidermal detachment • Discoloration (greenish-black) due to putrefaction gases and bacterial action • Blebs (fluid-filled vesicles) due to autolysis and bacterial activity

Other options:
Mummification (Option A): Occurs in dry, hot climates, leading to dehydration and leather-like skin, not blisters and blebs Burns (Option C): Cause erythema, charring, and coagulative necrosis, but do not typically produce decomposition-like blebs Adipocere (Option D): Refers to the saponification of body fat in moist, anaerobic conditions, producing a waxy, soap-like appearance, not blisters and skin slippage

q: A patient comes with blackish discolouration in the post auricular region. The sign is called
e:
D. Battle sign
Explanation
Battle Sign refers to blackish or bluish discoloration (ecchymosis) in the post-auricular region, which is highly suggestive of a basilar skull fracture, particularly involving the middle cranial fossa. It occurs due to blood tracking through the soft tissues from the fracture site

Other options:
A) Greisinger Sign: Seen in sigmoid sinus thrombosis, characterized by edema and tenderness over the mastoid due to venous congestion
B) Gradenigo Sign: A triad of otitis media, abducens nerve palsy, and retro-orbital pain, indicating petrous apicitis
C) Trotter triad: Associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma, presenting as trismus, pain, and conductive hearing loss due to involvement of the mandibular nerve

q: The maximum age of the person by the analysis of carpal bones in this X-ray is
e:
C. 10 years
Explanation
The carpal bones appear in a specific chronological order during skeletal maturation. The pisiform bone is the last carpal bone to ossify, usually appearing around 9-12 years of age. If the pisiform is absent in the X-ray, the maximum age of the person is likely 7 years

Other options:
At 5 years (A): Several other carpal bones have yet to ossify, but the pisiform is not expected at this stage 10 years (Option C): Pisiform usually appears by 9-12 years, so maximum age should be 7 years if it is absent At 13 years (D): The pisiform should be visible by this age in almost all individuals

q: Which of the following is first affected in rigor mortis
e:
B. Myocardium
Explanation
Rigor mortis is the postmortem stiffening of muscles due to depletion of ATP, leading to sustained muscle contraction. The myocardium is the first to undergo rigor mortis, but it is not externally visible Other Options: A) Eyelids: One of the first external muscles to show rigor, but not the absolute first C) Jaw: Also affected early, but follows the myocardium in rigor mortis progression D) Neck: Affected after the jaw and face muscles

q: Punishment for perjury is defined under section
e:
A. 193
Explanation
Perjury refers to giving false evidence under oath in a judicial proceeding. Section 191 IPC defines giving false evidence but does not specify the punishment Section 193 IPC specifically prescribes punishment for perjury, which includes • Imprisonment up to 7 years and a fine if perjury is committed in a judicial proceeding • Imprisonment up to 3 years and a fine if perjury is committed in any other case

Other options:
Section 191 IPC: Defines "Giving False Evidence" but does not state the punishment Section 197 IPC: Deals with prosecution of public servants, not perjury Section 190 IPC: Deals with magistrates taking cognizance of offenses, not perjury

q: Gastric lavage is not contraindicated after ingestion of
e:
C. Carbolic acid
Explanation
Gastric lavage is contraindicated in cases of corrosive poisoning (e.g., strong acids and alkalis) because it can cause further damage to the esophagus and stomach. However, in carbolic acid (phenol) poisoning, gastric lavage may be cautiously performed using glycerin or alcohol to neutralize and prevent further mucosal damage. Carbolic acid is less corrosive than mineral acids; gastric lavage can be performed cautiously with alcohol/glycerin

Other options:
A) Hydrochloric Acid: Strong corrosive acid that causes severe mucosal burns, perforation, and necrosis
B) Sulfuric Acid: Highly corrosive, causes severe dehydration and coagulative necrosis, leading to esophageal perforation
D) Nitric Acid: Strong oxidizing acid, causes deep tissue necrosis and perforation risk

q: Viscera in toxicology is stored in?
e:
B. Rectified spirit
Explanation
In forensic toxicology, viscera (organs like liver, stomach, intestine, etc.) are preserved in rectified spirit for chemical analysis of poisons • Preserves tissues and prevents decomposition • Does not interfere with chemical tests for most poisons (except alcohol and volatile poisons)

Other options:
Glycerine (Option A): Not used as it does not prevent decomposition effectively Formalin (Option C): Used for histopathology but not for toxicology (destroys poisons) Saturated salt solution (Option D): Used in organophosphate poisoning cases but not for routine toxicology

q: Identical twins will not have the same
e:
A. Fingerprints
Explanation
Identical (monozygotic) twins originate from a single fertilized egg that splits into two embryos, meaning they share 100% of their genetic material (DNA). However, they do not have identical fingerprints due to unique environmental influences during fetal development

Other options:
B) DNA copies: Identical twins have the same DNA sequence because they originate from the same zygote
C) Iris color: Determined by genetics, which is the same in identical twins
D) Blood group: Blood type is inherited from parents, and identical twins will have the same blood group

q: In alleged history of gun shot injury, there is burning, blackening, tattooing around the wound, dirt collar. The injury is
e:
A. Close shot entry wound
Explanation
Close shot entry wound: Burning, blackening, tattooing, and a dirt collar around the wound indicate a close-range gunshot entry wound. Tattooing occurs due to unburnt gunpowder embedding into the skin, while blackening and burning result from the hot gases expelled from the firearm. A dirt collar (abrasion collar) forms due to the bullet rubbing against the skin upon entry

Other options:
B) Close shot exit wound: Exit wounds do not exhibit burning, blackening, or tattooing because there is no direct contact with gunpowder or gases. Exit wounds are typically irregular in shape and larger than entry wounds due to the bullet's deformation and tumbling inside the body
C) Distant shot entry wound: Distant gunshot wounds lack blackening, burning, or tattooing since the gunpowder and heat dissipate before reaching the target. The entry wound at a distant shot is clean with an abrasion collar but no soot or tattooing
D) Distant shot exit wound: Like Close shot exit wounds, distant shot exit wounds also lack burning, blackening, and tattooing. They are irregular, everted, and larger than entry wounds, without the characteristic gunpowder effects

q: A child is having battered baby syndrome. How will you identify
e:
C. Bruises of different ages
Explanation
Battered baby syndrome (Child Abuse Syndrome) refers to non-accidental trauma in children due to physical abuse. A key diagnostic feature is the presence of bruises at different stages of healing, indicating repeated injuries over time

Other options:
A) Stab wound ? Not a typical injury in battered baby syndrome
B) Gunshot wound ? Rare in child abuse, more associated with criminal violence
D) None of these ? Incorrect, as bruises of different stages are a well-documented finding in child abuse

q: Degloving skin involves removal of?
e:
D. Skin, subcutaneous fat
Explanation
Degloving injuries occur when the skin and subcutaneous tissue are forcibly separated from the underlying structures, often due to high-impact trauma (e.g., road traffic accidents, industrial injuries) Degloving typically involves removal of skin and subcutaneous fat, exposing underlying fascia, muscle, or bone

Other options:
A) Skin, subcutaneous fat, fascia, muscle: Muscle is usually not removed in a degloving injury; it remains attached to deeper structures
B) Skin, subcutaneous fat, fascia: Fascia is usually intact
C) Skin only: Subcutaneous fat is also involved in degloving

q: In Indian judiciary which of the following represents Mc Naughten
e:
A. IPC 84
Explanation
McNaughten’s Rule is codified under Section 84 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). This section provides legal protection to individuals suffering from mental illness at the time of committing an offense. It states that a person cannot be held criminally responsible if they were incapable of understanding the nature of their act due to unsoundness of mind

Other options:
B) CRPC 84: The Code of Criminal Procedure (CRPC) primarily deals with procedural laws, not substantive laws like criminal responsibility. Section 84 does not exist in CRPC concerning McNaughten’s Rule
C) IPC 48: Section 48 of IPC does not relate to McNaughten’s Rule. IPC 84 is the relevant provision for insanity defense
D) CRPC 48: CRPC deals with the procedure of trials, arrests, and investigations. McNaughten’s Rule pertains to substantive criminal law (IPC 84), not procedural law (CRPC 48)

q: All of the following articles are related to child rights except?
e:
C. Article 42
Explanation
The Constitution of India includes several provisions for the protection and welfare of children. However, Article 24 is not directly related to child rights, but rather to prohibition of child labor in hazardous industries

Other options:
Article 45: Part of Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), ensuring free and compulsory education for children under 6 years Article 42: Mandates just and humane conditions for work, including maternity relief, which indirectly supports child welfare Article 39: Directs the state to ensure children are not abused and have opportunities for healthy development

q: Locard in forensic medicine is famous for?
e:
A. Exchange theory
Explanation
Dr. Edmond Locard is famous for his "Locard’s Exchange Principle" in forensic science. The principle states “Every contact leaves a trace.” This means that whenever two objects or individuals come into contact, there is a transfer of materials such as hair, fibers, fingerprints, or DNA. It is the foundation of forensic investigations, used in crime scene analysis

Other options:
B) Identification of Sex from Bones: Sex determination from bones is done using skeletal differences, especially the pelvis and skull. This falls under forensic anthropology
C) Calculation of Stature from Bones: Height estimation from bones is based on formulas like Trotter & Gleser’s method using the long bones (femur, tibia, humerus)
D) Estimation of Age: Age estimation in forensic medicine is done by examining teeth (dental eruption), bones (epiphyseal fusion), and skull sutures. This is studied in forensic odontology and anthropology, not Locard’s work

q: Which of the following causes bluish discoloration of stomach?
e:
D. Amytal
Explanation
Bluish discoloration of the stomach is most commonly seen with barbiturate poisoning, specifically Amytal (Amobarbital), which is a barbiturate. This occurs due to cyanosis and hypoxia: Barbiturates cause respiratory depression, leading to systemic hypoxia, which can result in bluish discoloration of mucosal surfaces, including the stomach. Congestion of gastric mucosa: Prolonged hypoxia can lead to vascular stasis and congestion, giving a bluish appearance to the stomach

Other options:
A) Arsenic: Causes hemorrhagic gastroenteritis but does not produce a bluish color
B) Lead: Causes lead lines (Burton's lines) on gums, abdominal colic, and neuropathy, but not blue stomach
C) Oxalic Acid: Causes corrosive gastritis with whitish or grayish mucosa due to calcium oxalate precipitation

q: Which of the following is first to putrefy?
e:
C. Brain
Explanation
The brain is the first organ to putrefy, especially in infants and individuals with high fever at death. This happens because it is high in moisture content and it has soft consistency compared to other organs. It is rich in blood supply, making it a good medium for bacterial growth. In warm and humid conditions, liquefaction of the brain occurs rapidly

Other options:
A) Heart resists putrefaction longer than the brain. It is a muscular organ with relatively lower water content, making decomposition slower
B) Kidney decomposes after the brain. They have moderate moisture content, but their compact structure delays putrefaction
D) Prostate is one of the last organs to putrefy due to dense fibrous tissue and lower water content. In forensic autopsy, the prostate and uterus are often the last organs to decompose

q: A patient presented with muscle pain and proximal tubular damage of nephrons. Which of the following is likely cause?
e:
D. Mercury
Explanation
Mercury toxicity, especially from inorganic mercury (Hg²?) compounds, can lead to • Muscle pain (myalgia): Due to mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress • Proximal tubular damage: Mercury accumulates in the proximal tubules of the nephron, causing acute tubular necrosis (ATN), proteinuria, and oliguria • Neurotoxicity: Chronic exposure leads to tremors, mood changes, and memory loss (Erethism mercurialis)

Other options:
A) Lead: Causes chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis, basophilic stippling, anemia, and neuropathy but is not the primary cause of acute proximal tubular damage
B) Cadmium: Primarily affects the proximal tubules, causing Fanconi-like syndrome, but it is not associated with muscle pain
C) Arsenic: Causes gastrointestinal symptoms, neuropathy, and Mees' lines but does not specifically damage the proximal tubules

q: Posthumous child is-
o: Born after death of both parent
e:
A. Born after death of father
Explanation
A posthumous child refers to a child who is born after the father has died. This can happen if the father dies while the mother is pregnant, and the child is born later. Such cases are significant in inheritance laws and legal rights of the child

Other options:
B) Born after the death of the mother: If the mother dies during pregnancy, the baby may be delivered via post-mortem C-section. However, this is not referred to as a posthumous child
C) Born after the death of both parents: There is no specific legal term for a child born after both parents have died. In such cases, the guardian or relatives take care of the child
D) Born dead: A baby that is born dead is called a stillbirth, not a posthumous child

q: The method of autopsy carried out en masse to remove from tongue to prostate is-
e:
D. Letulle technique
Explanation
Letulle method involves the en masse removal of all thoracic, cervical, abdominal, and pelvic organs as a single block. It allows for detailed examination of organ relationships and is commonly used in forensic autopsies

Other options:
Virchow method: Organs are removed one by one for individual examination Rokitansky method: In situ dissection of organs, removing them only after dissection Ghon method: Removal of organs in functional groups (thoracic, abdominal, and cervical)

q: A HIV positive patient died, and his body was brought for post mortem. The method of autopsy to be done is-
e:
D. Rokitanksy technique
Explanation
The Rokitansky autopsy method is commonly used for infectious disease cases, including HIV/AIDS, as it minimizes the risk of infection exposure to the pathologist

Other options:
A) Ghon Method: A limited autopsy method focusing on the lungs and is not used for full-body infectious disease cases
B) Letulle Method (En Masse Removal): Entire organ systems are removed together and dissected externally, which increases the risk of exposure to infectious material
C) Virchow Method (One-by-One Organ Removal): Each organ is removed separately, leading to higher aerosolization risks during dissection

q: A male child came to the casualty with difficulty in walking and pain in perianal region. On subjecting the specimen from the perianal region to a test, it produces yellow needle-shaped rhombic crystals with picric acid. What is the test done?
e:
A. Barberio test
Explanation
Barberio test: A test for the presence of spermatozoa, where picric acid reacts with spermine in semen to form yellow, needle-shaped, rhombic crystals. This is useful in forensic cases of sexual assault

Other options:
Florence test: Detects choline in semen, forming brown, needle-shaped crystals with iodine and potassium iodide Teichmann test: A confirmatory test for blood, forming brown rhombic crystals of hematin with glacial acetic acid and salt Acid phosphatase test: Used for detecting semen, but it does not produce crystalline formations

q: A patient was brought to the casualty with seizures. He had multiple episodes and was taking herbal medicines for the same. He was conscious in between the episodes. During the episodes, he had arching of his back. What is the likely cause?
e:
A. Strychnine
Explanation
The hallmark of strychnine poisoning is recurrent episodes of generalized muscle spasms with opisthotonus (arching of the back) while the patient remains conscious in between episodes

Other options:
B) Ricinus: Causes gastrointestinal symptoms (severe vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain) and multi-organ failure, but no seizures
C) Nerium odorum (Oleander Poisoning): Contains cardiac glycosides, leading to bradycardia, arrhythmias, and hyperkalemia, not opisthotonic seizures
D) Datura (Anticholinergic Toxicity): Causes dilated pupils, hallucinations, dry mouth, hyperthermia, but does not cause recurrent seizures with opisthotonus

q: Section 314 IPC deals with-
o: Causing miscarriage with the consent of the mother
Causing miscarriage without the consent of mother
Death of the mother by act done with the intent to cause miscarriage
Causing death of the unborn child by an act amounting to culpable homicide
e:
C. Death of the mother by act done with the intent to cause miscarriage
Explanation
Section 314 IPC pertains to cases where a person performs an act with the intention of causing a miscarriage, and the mother dies as a result of that act, whether or not she consented. The section applies even if the act was not intended to cause the mother’s death but resulted in it

Other options:
Section 312 IPC: Causing miscarriage with consent Section 313 IPC: Causing miscarriage without consent Section 315 IPC: Preventing a child from being born alive or causing its death after birth

q: The temperature of a body of a deceased person is found to be 39 degrees Celsius. Which of the following is the most probable reason?
e:
B. Septicemia
Explanation
In forensic medicine, a postmortem body temperature higher than normal (above 37°C) is most commonly due to septicemia or hyperpyrexial conditions before death Other Options: A) Cyanide poisoning: Typically causes rapid death and may lead to early postmortem cooling rather than hyperthermia C) Corrosive poisoning: Causes severe tissue damage (GI burns, perforation) but does not significantly elevate body temperature postmortem D) Intra-abdominal hemorrhage: Can lead to hypovolemic shock and death, but it does not cause postmortem hyperthermia

q: A farmer felt a sting on his leg. He saw something moving away quickly. He then got drowsy and was taken to the hospital. He developed pain around the site and continued to bleed profusely from the wound site. The wound became red with blisters. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
e:
A. Viper
Explanation
Viper bite (especially Russell’s viper or saw-scaled viper) is known to cause local pain, swelling, and blistering around the bite site. Hemorrhagic manifestations due to venom-induced disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Persistent bleeding from the wound due to coagulopathy and platelet dysfunction. Systemic symptoms like drowsiness, hypotension, and shock

Other options:
Cobra bite (B) typically causes neurotoxic effects such as ptosis, respiratory paralysis, but does not lead to extensive bleeding or blistering Wasp sting (C) and Scorpion sting (D) cause pain, local swelling, and allergic reactions but are not associated with extensive bleeding or blister formation

q: A case of road traffic accident was taken to mortuary for conducting post mortem examination. Who will authorize the autopsy?
e:
A. Police officer
Explanation
In cases of Road Traffic Accidents (RTA), the police officer investigating the case has the authority to request a medico-legal autopsy. This is done under Section 174 of the CrPC (Code of Criminal Procedure) in India to determine the cause of death. Other Options: B) Magistrate: A magistrate orders an autopsy in suspicious, custodial deaths, or exhumation cases. However, in routine RTA cases, the police officer’s authorization is sufficient C) Autopsy Surgeon: The autopsy surgeon (forensic expert) performs the postmortem but does not have the authority to order it. They act on the request of the police or magistrate D) Public Prosecutor: The public prosecutor is involved in legal proceedings after the postmortem is done but does not have the authority to request it

q: A man wearing female dress and high heels get sexual pleasure in doing. He was not attracted to the same gender. This condition is known as
e:
A. Transvestism
Explanation
Transvestism (Transvestic Fetishism) is a paraphilic disorder where a person derives sexual pleasure from wearing clothes of the opposite gender. However, they do not necessarily have gender dysphoria or same-sex attraction

Other options:
Voyeurism (B) refers to deriving sexual pleasure from watching others undress or engage in sexual activities without their knowledge Sexual dysphoria (C) (Gender Dysphoria) is a condition where a person feels distress due to a mismatch between their assigned gender and their experienced gender Gay orientation (D) refers to sexual attraction toward the same gender, which is not relevant here as the individual is not attracted to the same sex

q: Sequence of rigor mortis is
e:
B. Head to foot
Explanation
Rigor mortis follows a definite sequence in the body, progressing in a "head-to-foot" direction due to depletion of ATP and muscle contraction Sequence of Rigor Mortis: 1. Begins in small muscles (eyelids, jaw, neck) 2. Spreads to upper limbs (shoulders, arms, hands) 3. Progresses to the trunk and lower limbs 4. Finally affects the feet and toes This follows Nysten's rule, which states that rigor mortis progresses from head to toe due to the descending ATP depletion in muscles Other Options: A) Centre to periphery, as rigor does not start centrally; it begins in smaller muscles first C) Foot to head, as rigor starts in the head and moves downward D) Periphery to centre, as rigor moves sequentially downward, not from the periphery inward

q: Recording of evidence of a female in sexual assault case in court is done by
e:
C. In camera proceeding
Explanation
In camera proceedings (Option C) refer to legal proceedings conducted privately in a courtroom, away from the public and media, to protect the dignity and privacy of the victim, especially in sensitive cases like sexual assault. This ensures that the victim can testify without fear of social stigma or intimidation

Other options:
Option A (Open proceedings) is incorrect because general court cases are usually open to the public, but in sexual assault cases, the testimony is kept private Option B (Closed proceedings) is incorrect as it is a broader term. While sexual assault cases require privacy, "in camera" is the specific legal term used for such hearings Option D (With camera) is incorrect because it implies video recording, which is not mandatory or appropriate in sexual assault cases

q: Police brought a person from railway track with features of dry mouth, dilated pupil, dry skin, slurring of speech and delirium. It is case of ……………… poisoning.
e:
C. Datura
Explanation
The symptoms described in the clinical scenario are dry mouth, dilated pupils (mydriasis), dry skin, slurred speech, and delirium are characteristic of anticholinergic toxicity, which is classically seen in Datura poisoning Other Options: A) Morphine causes miosis (constricted pupils), respiratory depression, and drowsiness, which are opposite to the symptoms seen in this case B) Cocaine causes mydriasis, but it also leads to hyperactivity, tachycardia, chest pain, and hypertension, not delirium and dry mouth D) Alcohol can cause slurred speech and delirium, but it does not cause dry mouth, dry skin, or dilated pupils. Alcohol toxicity typically presents with CNS depression, ataxia, and respiratory depression in severe cases

q: Examination of a suspicious stain shows the following findings. The test is
e:
A. Barberio's test
Explanation
Barberio test (Option A) is a chemical test for sperm detection. It detects spermine, a component of seminal fluid, by reacting with picric acid to form yellow needle-shaped rhombic crystals

Other options:
Florence test (Option
B) is used to detect choline in seminal fluid, producing brown rhombic crystals (not yellow) Takayama test (Option
C) is a confirmatory test for blood, forming pyridine hemochromogen crystals (pinkish-red in color) Teichmann test (Option
D) is another blood test, producing brownish rhombic crystals when reacting with glacial acetic acid and salts

q: Child was born 8 months after death of father. The grandparents filed a case that the baby does not belong to their son. However, DNA came positive. What would you call the child as
e:
C. Posthumous child
Explanation
A posthumous child is a child who is born after the death of their biological father. This can occur due to • Natural conception before the father's death but birth occurring later • Artificial reproductive techniques (ART) such as sperm preservation and posthumous conception Other Options: A) Suppositious child: A child who is falsely claimed as someone's offspring (e.g., swapped at birth or falsely presented as an heir) B) Fabricated child: No such legal term; could imply an entirely fictional child D) Prehumous child: No such recognized term in medical or legal literature

q: Medicolegal examination of 18 year old man, who was accused of rape was done. During examination he states that he is 16 years old. Which joint x-ray should be done to determine age of the accused.
e:
C. Knee and wrist
Explanation
Determining age through radiology relies on epiphyseal fusion of bones. The most reliable joints for age estimation around 16–18 years include • Knee (Distal femur & Proximal tibia): Fusion occurs around 17–18 years • Wrist (Distal radius & ulna): Fusion occurs around 17–19 years

Other options:
A) Head and Shoulder: Not useful for age estimation around 16–18 years
B) Elbow and Ankle: Elbow fuses around 14–16 years, which may not confirm if he is above 16
D) Elbow and Hip: Hip fusion occurs later (~18–20 years), but the knee and wrist are more precise for this age range

q: A 14 year old victim of sexual assault with 22 weeks gestational age has been brought for MTP. True statement is:
o: MTP done in 2nd trimester only when mother’s life is in danger
MTP can be carried upto 24 weeks
MTP cannot be done more than 20 weeks
e:
C. MTP can be carried upto 24 weeks
Explanation
Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021, pregnancy can be terminated up to 24 weeks in cases involving minors, rape victims, incest, or other vulnerable groups Consent Requirements: • As she is below 18 years, guardian consent is mandatory (as per Section 3(4) of the MTP Act) • Additionally, because the pregnancy is beyond 20 weeks but within 24 weeks, two registered medical practitioners (RMPs) must approve the termination Mandatory Reporting: • Since this is a case of sexual assault, it falls under Protection of Children from Sexual Offenses (POCSO) Act, 2012 • The doctor must report the case to the police before proceeding with MTP

q: 27 weeks of gestation with congenital anomalies, whose presence is not required for authorization of MTP?
e:
B. Lawyer
Explanation
Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act, 2021 (India): For MTP beyond 24 weeks, a Medical Board is required, which includes • Obstetrician/Gynecologist • Pediatrician (to assess fetal viability and anomalies) • Sonologist/Radiologist (to confirm ultrasound findings) A lawyer is NOT a medical expert and is not required for authorization of MTP. The decision is based on medical criteria, not legal proceedings, unless there is a court order involved

q: Which chelating agent is not indicated in Iron overdose?
e:
B. BAL
Explanation
BAL (Dimercaprol) is not indicated for iron poisoning because it does not form stable complexes with iron. Instead, it is used for arsenic, mercury, lead, and gold poisoning

Other options:
Desferrioxamine is the chelator of choice for iron toxicity, as it specifically binds free iron and promotes its excretion Calcium EDTA is used for lead poisoning, not iron poisoning DTPA (Diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid) is mainly used for heavy metal poisoning, including plutonium and americium, but not for iron

q: The dead body shows the following finding as in the image what is the case
e:
D. Smothering
Explanation
Smothering is a form of mechanical asphyxia where external obstruction of the mouth and/or nose prevents breathing Key forensic findings in smothering: • Multiple abrasions around the nose and mouth (from struggle or pressure) • Petechial hemorrhages (due to asphyxia) • No ligature marks (which are seen in hanging or garotting)

Other options:
Hanging (A): Typically has a ligature mark on the neck, not abrasions on the nose/mouth Gagging (B): May involve foreign objects in the mouth, but does not cause multiple abrasions on the nose/mouth Garotting (C): Strangulation with a cord or wire, producing a deep horizontal ligature mark, not facial abrasions

q: Determine the range from the given image of entry wound of a rifled firearm
o: Cannot decide with the given information
e:
B. Close
Explanation
In rifled firearm injuries, the range of fire can be determined based on the appearance of the entry wound and surrounding effects such as • Contact wound: Soot deposition inside the wound, muzzle imprint, and tissue bursting • Close range wound: Presence of burns, tattooing (stippling), and soot deposition around the entry wound • Distant wound: Clean punched-out entry wound with no surrounding soot or tattooing Since the question specifies that the given image of the entry wound allows determination of range as "close," it suggests the presence of stippling and soot deposition around the wound but not the characteristics of a contact or distant wound

q: White waxy material with preserved facial feature is seen in dead body found in water. What is true about this condition.
o: It needs hot weather without humidity
Is a way of preservation by saponification of fats
e:
B. Is a way of preservation by saponification of fats
Explanation
The described condition is adipocere formation, which occurs due to the saponification (hydrolysis and hydrogenation) of body fat in moist environments, such as water or damp soil. The process results in a white, waxy, soap-like material that preserves body contours and facial features.

Other options:
A) It needs hot weather without humidity: Adipocere formation occurs in moist environments like water or wet soil. Hot and dry conditions promote mummification, not adipocere formation
C) Commonly occurs in non-fatty tissues: It primarily affects fatty tissues (e.g., cheeks, buttocks, breasts, thighs), as it involves fat hydrolysis
D) Occurs within minutes to hours: Adipocere formation takes weeks to months to develop. It is a slow process, requiring moisture and anaerobic condition

q: Which amongst the following is a true statement for diatoms
e:
B. Wall contains silica and chlorophyll
Explanation
Diatoms are microscopic unicellular algae (not bacteria) found in water bodies. They have silica-containing cell walls (frustules) and contain chlorophyll, enabling photosynthesis

Other options:
A) Microscopic unicellular bacteria: Diatoms are unicellular algae, not bacteria
C) Are resistant to acid: While organic parts of diatoms dissolve in strong acids, their silica walls remain intact, allowing forensic identification in drowning cases
D) Present only in bone marrow: Diatoms can be found in lungs, liver, spleen, and bone marrow in cases of antemortem drowning, but they are not exclusive to bone marrow

q: A patient came with complaints of nuchal rigidity, and altered consciousness. Lab reports shows tachypnea, hypotension, hypocalcemia, high anion gap acidosis. What is the diagnosis.
e:
B. Ethylene glycol
Explanation
Ethylene glycol (commonly found in antifreeze) is metabolized in the liver to toxic metabolites such as glycolic acid and oxalic acid, which cause high anion gap metabolic acidosis and hypocalcemia due to calcium oxalate crystal deposition • Nuchal rigidity and altered consciousness ? Suggest CNS involvement, common in ethylene glycol toxicity • Tachypnea ? Compensatory respiratory alkalosis due to metabolic acidosis • Hypotension ? Due to shock and metabolic toxicity • Hypocalcemia ? Due to precipitation of calcium oxalate crystals in tissues • High anion gap acidosis ? Due to accumulation of glycolic acid and oxalic acid

Other options:
A) Methyl alcohol (Methanol poisoning) causes optic nerve toxicity (blindness), metabolic acidosis, and CNS depression, but not hypocalcemia
C) Datura poisoning causes anticholinergic symptoms (mydriasis, tachycardia, hallucinations, dry skin), not metabolic acidosis or hypocalcemia
D) Digoxin toxicity causes hyperkalemia, bradycardia, visual disturbances (yellow-green vision), but not metabolic acidosis or hypocalcemia

q: Metabolites of methyl alcohol poisoning are
e:
A. Formic acid and lactic acid
Explanation
Methanol poisoning occurs due to its metabolism in the liver, leading to the production of toxic metabolites that cause severe metabolic acidosis and optic nerve toxicity Metabolism of Methanol: • Methanol ? Formaldehyde (via alcohol dehydrogenase) • Formaldehyde ? Formic acid (via aldehyde dehydrogenase) • Formic acid ? Causes metabolic acidosis, optic nerve damage, and blindness • Lactic acid accumulation also occurs due to tissue hypoxia from mitochondrial dysfunction

Other options:
B) Formic acid and oxalic acid: Formic acid is correct, but oxalic acid is a metabolite of ethylene glycol, not methanol
C) Oxalic acid and calcium oxalate: These are ethylene glycol metabolites, not methanol
D) Acetic acid and acetaldehyde: These are ethanol metabolites, not methanol

q: G5L4 woman has 4 daughters. She comes for USG examination and requests for sex determination of her fetus. What will you do?
o: Do USG check for congenital abnormality, gestational age and sex. But don’t tell the sex to mother
Do USG check for congenital abnormality, gestational age and sex. Tell sex to mother
Do USG-check for congenital abnormality, and gestational age. Don’t check for sex
e:
A. Do USG check for congenital abnormality, gestational age and sex. But don’t tell the sex to mother
Explanation
A) Check for congenital abnormality, gestational age, and sex, but don’t tell the sex to the mother: Ultrasound is done for medical indications (e.g., fetal anomalies, viability, growth). Sex determination may be incidentally noted but must not be disclosed as per the PCPNDT Act

Other options:
B) Check for congenital abnormality, gestational age, and sex, and tell the sex to the mother: Disclosing fetal sex is a criminal offense under the PCPNDT Act
C) Do USG, check for congenital abnormality and gestational age, but don’t check for sex: Fetal sex may be noted incidentally, even if the focus is on other parameters. The correct approach is to check but not disclose (Option
A)
D) Don’t do USG examination: Ultrasound is necessary for assessing fetal well-being. Refusing USG would be medical negligence

q: Protoporphyrin levels are elevated in which poisoning
e:
A. Lead
Explanation
Protoporphyrin levels, specifically Zinc Protoporphyrin (ZPP) and Free Erythrocyte Protoporphyrin (FEP), are elevated in lead poisoning due to lead’s interference with heme synthesis Lead inhibits the enzymes ferrochelatase and ?-ALA dehydratase, preventing iron incorporation into protoporphyrin IX. This leads to an accumulation of free protoporphyrin, which binds zinc instead of iron, forming zinc protoporphyrin (ZPP)

Other options:
B) Arsenic: Arsenic poisoning affects sulfhydryl-containing enzymes, but does not elevate protoporphyrins
C) Mercury: Mercury poisoning leads to neurological and renal toxicity, but does not impact protoporphyrin metabolism
D) Thallium: Thallium poisoning causes neuropathy, alopecia, and gastrointestinal symptoms, but does not affect protoporphyrin levels

q: Identify the poisoning based on the given images
e:
A. Arsenic
Explanation
The presence of Aldrich-Mees lines (transverse white bands on nails) and raindrop pigmentation (spotted hyperpigmentation on the skin) are hallmark features of chronic arsenic poisoning • Aldrich-Mees lines ? Arsenic disrupts keratin synthesis, leading to white bands on the nails that do not fade with pressure • Raindrop pigmentation ? Chronic exposure leads to patchy hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation, giving a raindrop appearance

Other options:
B) Thallium: Thallium poisoning causes Mees' lines, but not raindrop pigmentation. It is more associated with hair loss, painful neuropathy, and alopecia
C) Cocaine: Cocaine use does not cause these dermatological features. It is linked to cardiac arrhythmias, nasal septum perforation, and formication (cocaine bugs)
D) Cannabis: Cannabis use causes euphoria, conjunctival injection (red eyes), and increased appetite, but not nail or skin changes

q: A patient presents with tachycardia, mydriasis and diaphoresis. What could be the possible poisoning
e:
A. Cocaine
Explanation
The patient presents with tachycardia, mydriasis (dilated pupils), and diaphoresis (excessive sweating), which are classic sympathetic overstimulation features seen in cocaine toxicity Cocaine is a sympathomimetic drug that increases dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin levels by inhibiting their reuptake, leading to tachycardia, mydriasis (pupil dilation), diaphoresis (excessive sweating), hypertension, hyperthermia, and agitation

Other options:
B) Heroin is an opioid, which causes miosis (pinpoint pupils), respiratory depression, and sedation, opposite of the given symptoms
C) Morphine, another opioid, leading to miosis and bradypnea (slow breathing), not mydriasis and tachycardia
D) Cannabis causes conjunctival injection (red eyes), dry mouth, and euphoria, but not tachycardia, mydriasis, or diaphoresis

q: A pregnant lady, 37 weeks of gestation with labor pain presents to casualty. Emergency LSCS was done as there was no progress of labour. The gynecologist noted severe intractable hemorrhage after birth. Emergency hysterectomy was done in good faith to save life of the mother without consent. Which of the following is true.
o: Doctor not liable because he had to save her life in emergency
e:
A. Doctor not liable because he had to save her life in emergency
Explanation
In life-threatening emergencies, when the patient is unable to provide consent and immediate action is required to save their life, doctors are legally protected under the doctrine of "Necessity" or Emergency Exception • In this case, the patient had intractable hemorrhage, which is a life-threatening obstetric emergency • Emergency hysterectomy was performed in good faith to save her life • Consent is not required in life-threatening situations where delay in treatment could result in death

Other options:
B) Doctor is liable for negligence: There is no negligence because the procedure was medically necessary to prevent maternal death
C) Should have taken bedside consent: Ideally, consent should be taken, but in emergency cases, when the patient is unconscious or unable to consent, and no legal guardian is present, treatment must proceed immediately
D) None of the above: Option A is correct, so this option is not applicable

q: On ultrasound examination it was seen that there are twins, with an age difference of approximately one month. What is true of this scenario.
e:
A. Superfetation
Explanation
Superfetation refers to the fertilization and implantation of a second ovum during an ongoing pregnancy, leading to twins with a noticeable gestational age difference. This is extremely rare in humans but can occur when ovulation continues after conception, allowing fertilization at different times

Other options:
B) Superfecundation occurs when two ova from the same cycle are fertilized by sperm from different acts of intercourse. In this case, both fetuses would have the same age, unlike superfetation where there is a time gap
C) Posthumous child refers to a child born after the father’s death (e.g., sperm stored and used after the father’s demise). Not related to different gestational ages in twins
D) Prehumous child: No such medical term exists in this context

q: In Embryological development what causes release of testosterone from testes
e:
B. Hcg from placenta
Explanation
Hcg from placenta Release of testosterone- from fetal testes first β stimulus for testosterone release = HCG from placenta HCG – Imp. Points: • subunit = specific – used in preg. Test • Rescues C.L from Luteolysis • HCG – functionally & structurally similar to LH. • HCG maintains C.L of preg. (LH- maintains non preg. Corpus luteum) • Glycoprotein hormone • Max @ 10 wks. • Min @ 16 wks.

q: Which type of hymen is shown in the image below
e:
A. Septate
Explanation
Types of hymens: 1. Annular Hymen – A circular opening in the center of the membrane, the most common type. 2. Crescentic Hymen – A crescent-shaped opening, usually at the bottom of the vaginal opening. 3. Septate Hymen – The membrane has one or more bands of extra tissue that create multiple small openings instead of one. 4. Cribriform Hymen – A hymen with multiple small perforations, resembling a sieve. 5. Microperforate Hymen – A hymen with a very small opening, which can make menstruation and tampon use difficult. 6. Imperforate Hymen – A hymen that completely covers the vaginal opening, preventing menstrual blood from exiting and potentially requiring medical intervention. 7. Parous Introitus – This occurs after childbirth or sexual activity when the hymen is stretched, leaving remnants along the vaginal walls.

q: Contraception of choice for 18months postpartum woman who is breast feeding having heavy and irregular bleeding
e:
C. Mala n
Explanation
Mala n 1. Breastfeeding Impact: • At 18 months postpartum, breastfeeding is usually not the primary source of nutrition for the baby. • By this stage, the use of combined oral contraceptive pills (COCs) like Mala N is generally acceptable since the risk of estrogen reducing milk supply is lower. 2. Irregular, Heavy Bleeding: • Progestin-only methods (like norethisterone enanthate injection) can sometimes cause unpredictable bleeding. • COCs (Mala N) help regulate the cycle and reduce heavy bleeding, making it a good option. 3. Contraceptive Efficacy & Suitability: • Mala N (COC): Helps regulate bleeding and provides effective contraception. • Norethisterone Enanthate Injection: Progestin-only, but may cause irregular or prolonged spotting. • Progestasert IUD: Progesterone-based but not commonly used due to limited availability. • Copper T IUD: Non-hormonal, but can worsen heavy bleeding—not ideal in this case.

q: COPPER T contraindicated in
o: Post molar evacuation after trophoblastic disease
e:
C. Post molar evacuation after trophoblastic disease
Explanation
Post molar evacuation after trophoblastic disease 1. Absolute Contraindications (Should NOT be used) These conditions make Cu-IUD unsafe: 1. Pregnancy or suspected pregnancy 2. Unexplained vaginal bleeding (undiagnosed cause) 3. Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) (current or recurrent) 4. Active sexually transmitted infection (STI) (e.g., gonorrhea, chlamydia) 5. Puerperal sepsis (infection after childbirth) 6. Septic abortion (infection after miscarriage/abortion) 7. Severe uterine distortion or anomalies (e.g., bicornuate uterus, large fibroids) 8. Copper allergy or Wilson’s disease (excess copper storage disorder) 9. Endometrial or cervical cancer 10. Recent pelvic tuberculosis 11. Post-molar pregnancy evacuation (until hCG normalizes to rule out persistent trophoblastic disease)

q: 22 year old female presents with infertility. HSG was done what is your diagnosis
e:
D. Septate
Explanation
Septate Diagnostic Imaging Findings 1. Hysterosalpingography (HSG), screening only • Septate uterus ? Narrow, symmetric endometrial cavities • Bicornuate uterus ? Broad, separate cavities with fundal cleft 2. 3D Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVS), IOC • Septate uterus ? Flat/concave external fundal contour • Bicornuate uterus ? Convex or notched external fundus 3. MRI (Most Accurate) • Septate uterus ? Fibrous (low T2 signal) or muscular midline septum • Bicornuate uterus ? Two widely spaced endometrial cavities with a clear fundal cleft 4. Hysteroscopy + Laparoscopy (Gold Standard for Confirmation) • Septate uterus ? Normal external uterine shape with an internal fibrous band • Bicornuate uterus ? Visible external fundal indentation and separate horns

q: Recommendation after surgery for VVF
o: Abstinence for 3 weeks avoid pregnancy for 2 years
Abstinence for 3 months avoid pregnancy for 1 year
Abstinence for 6 weeks avoid pregnancy for 6 years
Abstinence for 6 months avoid pregnancy for 1 year
e:
B. Abstinence for 3 months avoid pregnancy for 1 year
Explanation
Abstinence for 3 months avoid pregnancy for 1 year Abstinence After VVF Repair • Recommended Duration: 3–6 months • Reason: • Allows complete healing of the surgical site. • Reduces risk of infection and fistula recurrence. • Prevents excessive pressure on the repaired area. Pregnancy Avoidance Guidelines • Minimum Time Before Conception: At least 12–24months • Reason: • Ensures full tissue recovery and strength before pregnancy. Delivery Plan for Future Pregnancies • Mode of Delivery: Elective Cesarean Section (C-Section) is recommended in most cases. • Why? • Prevents excessive pressure on the repaired area. • Reduces risk of fistula recurrence. • Vaginal delivery is generally NOT recommended, especially if the original fistula was due to obstructed labor. • Reduces risk of fistula recurrence during pregnancy or labor. • Decreases risk of urinary incontinence or bladder dysfunction.

q: Which of the following is not used as an emergency contraception?
e:
A. Danazole
Explanation
1. Danazol (A) – Not Used for Emergency Contraception • Danazol is a synthetic androgen that suppresses ovulation by inhibiting gonadotropins. • It is used mainly for endometriosis, fibrocystic breast disease, and hereditary angioedema. • It does not function as an emergency contraceptive. 2. Copper T IUD (B) – Used for Emergency Contraception • Can be inserted within 5 days of unprotected intercourse. • Prevents fertilization by creating a spermicidal intrauterine environment. • Most effective form of emergency contraception (>99% efficacy). 3. RU-486 (Mifepristone) (C) – Used for Emergency Contraception • Anti-progesterone that prevents implantation and disrupts early pregnancy. • Can be used in low doses (25-50 mg) as emergency contraception. • Also used for medical abortion in higher doses. 4. High-Dose Estrogen (D) – Used for Emergency Contraception • Previously used as Yuzpe regimen (ethinyl estradiol + high-dose progestin). • Works by inhibiting ovulation and altering the endometrium. • Less commonly used today due to nausea and lower efficacy compared to newer methods.

q: First line of Rx of osteoporosis in post menopausal women:
e:
B. Bisphophonaes
Explanation
Bisphosphonates are TOC for osteoporosis in post menopausal women Post menopausal HRT. Is usually started for either HOT flashes or vaginal atrophy. For Hot flashes, systemic trans dermal > oral. For vaginal atrophy, local estrogen application. SERM – not used for mx of ‘Hot flushes’ because S/E itself is not flushes.

q: Which of the following is not estrogen dependent pubertal change:
e:
A. Hair growth
Explanation
Estrogen-Dependent Pubertal Changes: 1. Breast development (Thelarche) 2. Growth spurt & epiphyseal plate closure 3. Fat redistribution & body shape changes 4. Uterine and vaginal maturation 5. Menarche (first period) 6. Skin softening & decreased acne 7. Cardiovascular benefits (higher HDL, lower LDL) Pubic Hair (Pubarche) ? Androgen-dependent • Initiated by adrenal androgens (DHEA, DHEA-S, androstenedione). • Starts around Tanner Stage 2-3, occurring after thelarche in females. 2. Axillary (Armpit) Hair ? Androgen-dependent • Begins after pubic hair development, driven by adrenal androgens. 3. Facial and Body Hair ? Androgen-dependent • In females, low androgen levels result in fine, sparse facial hair. • In males, higher testosterone ? DHT conversion leads to dense beard growth.

q: Identify the image:
e:
B. B/L Hydrosalpinx
Explanation
Bilateral hydrosalpinx = Both fallopian tubes blocked with fluid. ? PID, endometriosis, TB, and past surgery are common causes. ? Main symptom = Infertility (often asymptomatic otherwise). ? Diagnosed via ultrasound, HSG, or laparoscopy. ? Treatment = Surgery (salpingectomy) + IVF for fertility. Natural conception is unlikely if both tubes are completely blocked. • IVF (In Vitro Fertilization) is the best option for achieving pregnancy. • Salpingectomy before IVF improves success rates by removing the inflammatory fluid that can reduce embryo implantation.

q: Secondary wave of trophoblastic invasion
o: Invasion of radial artery by cytotrophoblast
Invasion of arcuate artery by cytotrophoblast
Invasion od spiral artery by villous trophoblast
Invasion of spiral artery by extravillous trophoblast
e:
D. Invasion of spiral artery by extravillous trophoblast
Explanation
The secondary wave of trophoblastic invasion is a critical event during normal placental development in the first half of pregnancy. It ensures proper vascular remodeling of the maternal spiral arteries, which is essential for adequate uteroplacental blood flow to support the growing fetus. Process of Secondary Trophoblastic Invasion 1. Timing: • Occurs between 12–20 weeks of gestation, following the initial wave of trophoblastic invasion during implantation (6–12 weeks). 2. Role of Extravillous Trophoblasts (EVTs): • Cytotrophoblasts differentiate into extravillous trophoblasts (EVTs), which invade the maternal spiral arteries and interstitial areas of the decidua and myometrium. 3. Mechanism: • The EVTs invade and remodel the maternal spiral arteries, replacing the endothelium and vascular smooth muscle cells. • This process converts the small, high-resistance spiral arteries into large, low-resistance vessels capable of delivering high volumes of maternal blood to the placenta. 4. Extent of Invasion: • The secondary wave extends into the decidua basalis and deeper into the myometrial portion of the spiral arteries. • It provides sustained blood flow to meet the demands of the rapidly growing fetus. Key Functions 1. Increased Uteroplacental Perfusion: • Ensures low-resistance, high-volume blood flow to the placenta, critical for oxygen and nutrient delivery. 2. Protection Against Hypoxia: • Prevents placental ischemia and hypoxia, which can adversely affect fetal development. Pathophysiology of Failed Secondary Invasion If the secondary wave of trophoblastic invasion is incomplete or fails: 1. Placental Dysfunction: • The spiral arteries remain narrow and high-resistance, leading to inadequate perfusion. 2. Associated Conditions: • Preeclampsia: Placental hypoxia and oxidative stress contribute to systemic endothelial dysfunction. • Fetal Growth Restriction (FGR): Insufficient placental blood flow restricts fetal growth. • Placental Abruption: Poor placental attachment and blood flow increase the risk of abruption. 3. Histological Findings: • Retention of smooth muscle and endothelium in spiral arteries. • Insufficient EVT invasion into the myometrial segment of the spiral arteries.

Implantation at the Internal Os (Placenta Previa): • Implantation at or near the internal os can lead to placenta previa, where the placenta partially or completely covers the cervix. • As the pregnancy progresses and the lower uterine segment stretches (particularly in the third trimester), the placenta may shear from its attachment site, causing painless but significant vaginal bleeding. • Bleeding Risk: • This is the most likely site of implantation to cause severe vaginal bleeding, as the lower uterine segment is poorly adapted for hemostasis due to its thin musculature. 2. Implantation at the Ovary: • Ovarian implantation is a rare form of ectopic pregnancy. • While it may cause intraperitoneal bleeding due to ovarian rupture, it is less likely to cause significant vaginal bleeding compared to implantation near the internal os. 3. Implantation in the Tube (Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy): • Tubal pregnancy is the most common site of ectopic pregnancy. • Rupture of the tube causes intraperitoneal hemorrhage, leading to abdominal pain and hemodynamic instability. • Vaginal bleeding is usually minimal and is secondary to hormonal changes, not direct hemorrhage. 4. Implantation in the Abdominal Cavity: • Abdominal pregnancy is a rare ectopic pregnancy. • Bleeding in this situation is usually intraperitoneal, not vaginal, and arises from detachment of the implanted trophoblastic tissue. Why Internal Os Causes Maximum Vaginal Bleeding • The internal os is located in the lower uterine segment, which: • Has poor contractility, making it less capable of stopping bleeding. • Contains large vascular sinuses that bleed profusely when disrupted. • Bleeding is directly vaginal due to the proximity to the cervix.

q: Absolute contraindication for cervical cerclage in patient with cervix 1.8cm
e:
C. Ruptured membranes
Explanation
Absolute Contraindications of cervical cerclage 1. Active Preterm Labor: • Presence of regular uterine contractions or advanced cervical dilation (beyond 4 cm) makes cerclage ineffective. 2. Intrauterine Infection (Chorioamnionitis): • Cerclage in the presence of infection increases the risk of sepsis and preterm rupture of membranes (PROM). 3. Ruptured Membranes (PROM): • Placement of cerclage in a setting of ruptured membranes increases the risk of infection and preterm delivery. 4. Significant Vaginal Bleeding: • Associated with conditions like placenta previa, where cerclage can exacerbate the situation. 5. Fetal Demise: • Cerclage is contraindicated if the fetus is non-viable. 6. Fetal Anomalies Incompatible with Life: • Cerclage is not appropriate when the pregnancy is unlikely to result in a live birth. 7. Uterine Contractions: • Active uterine contractions indicate labor, and cerclage at this stage may lead to complications. 8. Placental Abruption: • Active placental separation increases maternal and fetal risks, and cerclage is contraindicated.

q: Uterine artery doppler at 12-14 weeks can detect
e:
B. Early onset PE
Explanation
Doppler Findings: • Increased pulsatility index (PI): • Reflects high resistance in uterine arteries. • Notching: • A diastolic notch indicates incomplete remodeling of the spiral arteries and persistent vascular resistance. Screening with Uterine Artery Doppler 1. Timing: • Performed at 11-13+6 weeks during the first-trimester combined screening for aneuploidy. • Doppler is often combined with maternal factors and biomarkers like PlGF (placental growth factor) and sFlt-1 (soluble FMS-like tyrosine kinase-1) to enhance predictive accuracy. 2. Cutoffs for Risk Prediction: • Pulsatility Index (PI): • Elevated PI (?95th percentile for gestational age) indicates a higher risk of preeclampsia. • Bilateral Notching: • Presence of a persistent diastolic notch in both uterine arteries is strongly associated with early-onset preeclampsia.

q: After 7 weeks for MTP drugs used
e:
D. Mifepristone and misoprostol
Explanation
Medical Termination of Pregnancy After 7 Weeks (Up to 9 Weeks) 1. Drug Protocol: • Mifepristone: • Dosage: 200 mg orally. • Mechanism: Blocks progesterone receptors, causing detachment of the gestational sac. • Misoprostol: • Dosage: 800 mcg (4 tablets of 200 mcg each) vaginally or buccally 24–48 hours after mifepristone administration. • Mechanism: Induces uterine contractions to expel the pregnancy. 2. Gestational Limit: • Medical abortion using mifepristone and misoprostol is approved for up to 9 weeks of gestation (63 days) as per GOI guidelines. Key Points About MTP Act (2021 Amendment) • The gestational limit for abortion has been extended to 24 weeks for specific categories of women (e.g., survivors of rape, incest, or those with fetal anomalies). • Medical abortion with mifepristone and misoprostol is permitted up to 9 weeks of gestation under medical supervision. • After 9 weeks, surgical methods are generally preferred.

q: Which of the following is correct calorie requirement in 12 weeks pregnant woman
e:
B. 400 in third trimester
Explanation
Put this Explanation (GOI Guidelines on Calorie Requirements in Pregnancy) 1. Calorie Requirements by Trimester • First Trimester: • No significant increase in calorie requirements is needed because fetal growth is minimal during this period. A balanced diet is sufficient. • Additional calories: Minimal to none (around 0–100 kcal/day). • Second Trimester: • Energy requirements begin to rise due to fetal growth and increased maternal metabolic demands. • Additional calories: ~350 kcal/day. • Third Trimester: • The most significant increase in caloric needs occurs during this period due to rapid fetal growth and preparation for lactation. • Additional calories: ~400 kcal/day. Key Point from GOI Guidelines: The National Institute of Nutrition (NIN) and Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MOHFW), India, recommend an additional 350–400 kcal/day during pregnancy, with the largest increase in the third trimester.

q: After 5 days of vaginal delivery a woman brought to the casualty at 11pm by her husband with history of crying, loss of appetite difficulty in sleeping and feeling low self esteem. Her physical examination is unremarkable and no worrisome findings on pelvic examination. Which of the following is the best term to describe her symptoms
e:
A. Post partum Blues
Explanation
Postpartum Blues (Baby Blues) Postpartum blues is a transient mood disturbance experienced by many women shortly after childbirth, characterized by emotional instability and mild depressive symptoms. Key Features • Onset: Typically begins 2–3 days postpartum. • Duration: Lasts up to 10 days, resolving spontaneously without treatment. • Symptoms: • Mood swings • Tearfulness without a clear reason • Irritability • Anxiety • Fatigue • Difficulty concentrating • Prevalence: Affects up to 50–80% of new mothers. Etiology • Hormonal changes (e.g., rapid drop in estrogen and progesterone). • Physical and emotional stress of childbirth. • Sleep deprivation. • Adjustment to new maternal responsibilities. Management • Reassurance: Symptoms are self-limiting and normal. • Support: Emotional and practical support from family and friends. • Monitor: If symptoms persist beyond 2 weeks or worsen, evaluate for postpartum depression. Distinction from Postpartum Depression • Postpartum blues is mild and short-lived, while postpartum depression is more severe, lasts longer, and requires intervention.

q: A pimigravida is brought by her relatives after 1hr of full term vaginal delivery. Baby is doing well. On examination patient is hypotensive hypoxic and has DIC. She was previously normal with no known cardiac condition. Which of the following is the likely cause
e:
D. AFE
Explanation
Amniotic Fluid Embolism (AFE) Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare but catastrophic obstetric emergency characterized by the entry of amniotic fluid, fetal cells, or debris into the maternal circulation, triggering a severe systemic inflammatory response. Key Features • Incidence: 1–12 per 100,000 deliveries. • Onset: Sudden, during labor, cesarean section, or immediately postpartum. • Phases: 1. Cardiopulmonary collapse: • Sudden hypotension • Respiratory distress • Hypoxemia • Cardiac arrest 2. Coagulopathy: • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) • Massive hemorrhage • Uterine atony Symptoms • Sudden shortness of breath. • Hypotension or shock. • Seizures or altered mental status. • Cyanosis. • Severe bleeding (due to DIC). Diagnosis • Clinical diagnosis (no specific test). • Suspected based on sudden onset of cardiopulmonary collapse or DIC without other explanations. Management 1. Immediate Resuscitation: • ABCs (Airway, Breathing, Circulation). • Administer oxygen and intubate if necessary. • Initiate aggressive fluid resuscitation and vasopressors for shock. 2. Management of Coagulopathy: • Replace blood products (PRBCs, FFP, platelets, cryoprecipitate). 3. Supportive Care: • Transfer to ICU if stabilized. • Emergency delivery of the fetus if needed. Prognosis • Maternal mortality: 20–60%. • Survivors may experience neurological deficits or multi-organ failure. • Prompt recognition and management are critical for survival.

q: What condition in the mother associated with following fetal abnormally:
e:
B. DM
Explanation
Causal regression syndrome or sacral agenesis Key Features 1. Etiology: • Strongly associated with poorly controlled pregestational diabetes (hyperglycemia in the first trimester). • Hyperglycemia disrupts early embryogenesis, specifically affecting the caudal mesoderm. 2. Incidence: • More common in infants of diabetic mothers (1 in 350–500 diabetic pregnancies). • Rare in non-diabetic pregnancies. 3. Spectrum of Anomalies: • Partial to complete agenesis of the sacrum and lumbar spine. • Malformations of the pelvis and lower extremities (e.g., contractures, clubfoot). • Urinary and fecal incontinence due to neurogenic bladder or bowel dysfunction. • May include tethered cord or anomalies of the genitalia.

q: A 24 years old women who had home delivery 2 weeks back, now presents with complete perineal tear. What’s the next line of the management?
e:
A. Repair immediately
Explanation
Early Repair of Complete Perineal Tears 1. Timing: • Repairs performed at 2–3 weeks postpartum are increasingly recognized as safe and effective. • This approach may reduce prolonged discomfort, improve quality of life, and address symptoms such as fecal incontinence sooner. 2. Why Early Repair? • Improved healing: Early repair takes advantage of the post-delivery state when tissues are still vascular and pliable, promoting good wound healing. • Reduced complications: Delaying repairs for months increases the risk of scarring, fibrosis, and poor surgical outcomes. • Faster symptom relief: Early intervention addresses incontinence and pain more quickly, improving maternal well-being. Criteria for Early Repair Early repair (2–3 weeks postpartum) can be performed if: 1. No infection: • The site is clean with no active infection or purulent discharge. 2. Good tissue condition: • Edges of the tear are pliable and well-vascularized. 3. Maternal health: • The mother is stable and can tolerate surgery under local, regional, or general anesthesia
