Twitching motility is seen on wet saline mount Trichomonas vaginalis has a jerky or twitching type of mobility on wet saline mount. T. vaginalis has only stage in its life cycle i/e, trophozoite form (no cyst stage is seen). It is an obligate parasite and sexual transmission is the main route of infection. It produces the appearance of “strawberry cervix” due to petechial hemorrhages. The gold standard for diagnosis is culture on CPLM medium or PEM medium.

q: A lady from West Rajasthan presented with an ulcer surrounded by erythema on the right leg. Microscopy of the biopsy from the edge of the ulcer showed organisms with dark staining nuclei and kinetoplast. What is the most likely causative organism?
e:
A. Leishmania tropica
Explanation
Leishmania tropica The above clinical scenario is suggestive of cutaneous Leishmaniasis Leishmaniasis is caused by protozoa of genus Leishmania. It is transmitted by the bite of female Phlebotomus sandfly. It is endemic to Bihar, Jharkhand and Uttar Pradesh. The lifecycle of Leishmania includes two forms: Promastigote (in sandfly vector) and Amastigote (in the reticuloendothelial cells of the host). The amastigote form is also known as Leishmania-Donovan (LD) body. It is an intracellular form and it contains a kinetoplast.

q: A child presents with a fever and a rash. Urine examination showed cells with owl’s eye appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
A. Cytomegalovirus
Explanation
Cytomegalovirus Based on owls eye appearance on urinary examination, the most likely causative agent is cytomegalovirus. It causes infectious mononucleosis-like infection such as fever and rash in immunocompetent individuals, and a disseminated CMV infections like pneumonitis and colitis in immunosuppressed individuals. CMV spreads through contact with salivary secretions and sexual contact, blood transfusion and organ transplantation. A characteristic intranucleus basophilic inclusion surrounded by a clear halo is known as owl’s eye appearance.

q: Infection with Clonorchis sinensis is associated with an increased risk of-
e:
B. Cholangiocarcinoma
Explanation
Cholangiocarcinoma Clonorchis sinensis or Chinese liver fluke causes Clonorchiasis. It is associated with an increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma. Humans are infected by eating raw or undercooked fish containing encysted larvae (metacercariae).

q: A patient presented with complaints of persistent cough and weight loss. He had a history of contact with multiple sexual partners. He was diagnosed with HIV positive 6 months back and is poorly adherent to his medications. The fungal culture of sputum was negative. On Gomori methamine silver staining, the cells showed darkly stained crescent shaped cysts. What is the most likely causative organism?
e:
D. Pneumocystis jirovecii
Explanation
Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PcP) is an opportunistic infection in immunocompromised patients. It usually occurs when the CD4 count falls below 200cells/microlitre. Patients present with shortness of breath, fever and non-productive cough. CXR shows diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Gomori methamine silver stain shows black crescent shaped cysts resembling crushed ping-pong balls.

q: Which of the following laboratory test is used to diagnose rotavirus diarrhea?
o: Antigen detection in the stool sample
e:
A. Antigen detection in the stool sample
Explanation
Antigen detection in the stool sample Rotavirus is the most common cause of viral diarrhea in children below the age of 5 years. Most of the cases are asymptomatic or with mild symptoms like watery diarrhea, vomiting, low grade fever and temporary lactose intolerance. Diagnosis can be made by rapid antigen detection of rotavirus in stool specimens. EIA and PCR are used to detect the virus in stool. Treatment is supportive (correction of fluid and electrolyte imbalance).

q: A boy presented with fever and chills. Rapid test was positive for specific antigen HRP-2. Which of the following species of Plasmodium is the most likely causative agent?
e:
A. Plasmodium falciparum
Explanation
Plasmodium falciparum HRP-2 positivity is suggestive of P. falciparum malaria. Malaria is a parasitic infection caused by Plasmodium species transmitted by Anopheles mosquito. The new rapid antigen tests employ immunochromatographic methods. The parasite-F test is an example of one, that is based on the detection of Histidine-rich protein 2 (HRP-2) that is produced only by the asexual forms of plasmodium falciparum. Another diagnostic test detects lactate dehydrogenase (LDH test) that is positive for all Plasmodium species.

q: A child was brought with complaints of high fever, multiple seizures, headache and rigidity. CSF analysis showed low glucose, high protein, and many polymorphs. The CSF culture showed pleomorphic gram-negative bacilli. What is true about the causative organism?
o: Produces non-lactose fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar
Exhibits satellitism around Staph aureus colonies
It exhibits alpha hemolysis on sheep blood agar
e:
C. Exhibits satellitism around Staph aureus colonies
Explanation
Exhibits satellitism around Staph aureus colonies The case scenario is suggestive of meningitis caused by Hemophilus influenzae, which is a gram negative pleomorphic bacillus that is non-motile and non-spore forming. It exhibits satellitism around Staph aureus colonies. Bacitracin sensitivity is characteristic of Streptococcus pyogenes. Alpha hemolysis is characteristic of Streptococcus pneumoniae. Non-lactose fermenting colonies on MacConkey are associated with Shigella, Salmonella, and Proteus species.

q: A patient presented with high fever, altered sensorium, headache, neck rigidity and seizures. He was diagnosed with HSV encephalitis. Which of the following tests can be used to confirm the diagnosis?
o: CSF culture on chick embryo lines
e:
C. CSF PCR for viral DNA
Explanation
CSF PCR for viral DNA HSV DNA demonstration in CSF by PCR is the investigation of choice for HSV encephalitis. HSV encephalitis usually presents with acute onset of fever, altered level of consciousness, focal or diffuse neurologic signs and symptoms especially in the temporal lobe.

q: In a patient presented with a fever and a positive filarial antigen test, what is the next appropriate method of management?
o: Detection of microfilariae in the blood smear
e:
C. Detection of microfilariae in the blood smear
Explanation
Detection of microfilariae in the blood smear A patient with fever and filarial antigen positive is suggestive of filariasis. The next most appropriate step for this patient is detection of microfilariae in the blood smear. The microfilariae circulate in the blood at night showing a nocturnal periodicity, so blood smears of samples obtained at night between 10PM to 2AM can detect microfilariae. DEC provocation test refers to administration of DEC and subsequently collecting blood samples. Although DEC provocation has the advantage of blood sample collection even in the day time, guidelines suggest blood sample collection at night followed by identification of microfilariae in a blood smear.

q: A man presents with a history of dysuria and urethral discharge after having unprotected sexual intercourse. Gram staining of the purulent discharge is seen in the following image. What is the treatment of choice for this infection?
e:
C. Ceftriaxone
Explanation
Ceftriaxone The given clinical scenario along with microscopic findings of gram negative intracellular diplococci indicates infection with Neisseria gonorrhea. The treatment of choice for the infection is single-agent therapy with ceftriaxone. Gonorrhea is acquired by sexual contact. Symptoms include purulent urethral discharge and dysuria. Rarely, peritonitis may develop with perihepatic inflammation (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome).

q: Identify
e:
B. Pseudoexfoliation
Explanation
Pseudoexfoliation Syndrome (PEX) is a systemic condition that primarily affects the eye. It is characterized by the accumulation of extracellular fibrillar material on the anterior lens capsule, pupillary margin, and other intraocular structures. Due to weak zonular fibers, it is associated with an increased risk of glaucoma (pseudoexfoliation glaucoma) and complications during cataract surgery

Other options:
A) Vossius ring is a ring-shaped pigment deposition on the anterior lens capsule, usually due to blunt trauma. It forms from iris pigment epithelial cells that are transferred onto the lens
C) Foreign body: A retained intraocular foreign body would appear as a discrete object within the eye, often metallic or glass, rather than a diffuse flaky deposition
D) Ocular trauma: Trauma can lead to various changes in the eye (e.g., Vossius ring, hyphae, lens dislocation), pseudoexfoliation is a degenerative condition unrelated to acute injury

q: Which Vitamin deficiency cause this
e:
A. Vitamin A
Explanation
The given image shows Bitot’s spots. Bitot spots are foamy, keratinized plaques on the conjunctiva, often found bilaterally. They are caused by Vitamin A deficiency and are an early sign of xerophthalmia, which can progress to night blindness and corneal ulceration if untreated.

Other options:
B) Vitamin B – Various B-vitamin deficiencies cause neuropathy, anemia, and glossitis but not Bitot spots
C) Vitamin C – Deficiency leads to scurvy, characterized by gum bleeding, poor wound healing, and bruising
D) Vitamin D – Deficiency causes rickets (in children) and osteomalacia (in adults), affecting bone mineralization

q: The procedure is done for?
e:
B. Keratoconus
Explanation
Intracorneal Ring Segments (ICRS) are implanted in the corneal stroma to improve corneal shape and vision in patients with keratoconus

Other options:
A) Keratoglobus – A rare condition with generalized corneal thinning, usually not treated with ICRS but rather with protective measures or corneal graft
C) Vogt's Limbal Girdle – An age-related benign degenerative change at the corneal periphery, not requiring ICRS
D) Corneal Dystrophy – A group of inherited disorders affecting the cornea, often treated with corneal transplants or laser procedures, not ICRS

q: A diabetic patient with 6/9 visual acuity in 1 eye with retinal hemorrageswith neovascularization at optic disc. What is the management?
e:
B. Pan-retinal photocoagulation
Explanation
The presence of retinal hemorrhages and neovascularization of the optic disc (NVD) in a diabetic patient suggests proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR). Pan retinal photocoagulation (PRP) is the standard treatment to reduce the risk of vitreous hemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment

Other options:
A) Focal Laser Photocoagulation: Used for clinically significant macular edema (CSME)
C) Grid Laser: Used for diffuse diabetic macular edema (DME)
D) Scleral Buckling: Used for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD), not diabetic retinopathy

q: Parents brought their child to the clinic where he was found to have mental retardation, skeletal muscle weakness and cherry red spot in retina. What could be the diagnosis among the following?
e:
A. Tay-Sachs
Explanation
The child presents with mental retardation, skeletal muscle weakness, and cherry-red spots in the retina, which are characteristic features of Tay-Sachs disease, a lysosomal storage disorder caused by a deficiency of hexosaminidase A

Other options:
B) Hurler Syndrome: caused by alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency, leading to mucopolysaccharide accumulation and clinical features include Gargoylism, corneal clouding, skeletal abnormalities, and hepatosplenomegaly
C) Hunter Syndrome: Iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency leads to mucopolysaccharide buildup. No corneal clouding and it is X-linked inheritance
D) Gaucher Disease: Caused by glucocerebrosidase deficiency, leading to glucocerebroside accumulation in macrophages. Hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain, and anemia, but not cherry-red spots

q: A middle aged female with Rheumatoid arthritis presents with the following slit lamp picture. What is the condition shown here?
e:
B. Ciliary staphyloma
Explanation
Ciliary staphyloma is a local bulging or outpouching of the sclera around the limbus, often associated with chronic inflammation, such as in rheumatoid arthritis. This condition typically results in a thinning of the scleral tissue that may form a conical shape or bulge

Other options:
A) Scleromalacia Perforans: Chronic scleral thinning leading to perforation, often in rheumatoid arthritis and characterized by progressive weakening of the sclera without noticeable inflammation, leading to risk of scleral perforation
C) Melanoma: Malignant tumor originating from melanocytes and usually presents as pigmented lesion on the uveal tract, not associated with scleral bulging
D) Tranta Dots: Small white dots at the limbus seen in allergic conjunctivitis and it is Indicative of eosinophilic infiltration rather than scleral changes

q: Sympathetic ophthalmia would lead to?
e:
A. Panuveitis
Explanation
Sympathetic ophthalmia is a rare bilateral granulomatous uveitis that occurs after penetrating trauma to one eye, leading to inflammation of all layers of both eyes. It typically presents with panuveitis, which involves inflammation of the anterior, posterior, and intermediate uveal structures of both eyes

Other options:
B) Acute Anterior Uveitis primarily affects the anterior segment of the eye, such as the iris and ciliary body. This is not characteristic of sympathetic ophthalmia, which involves inflammation of all layers of the eye.
C) Chronic Anterior Uveitis is typically a persistent, low-grade inflammation of the anterior segment, but sympathetic ophthalmia causes a more acute and bilateral inflammation, not confined to the anterior segment
D) Posterior Uveitis involves inflammation of the choroid and retina, which may be seen in other conditions but is not the predominant feature in sympathetic ophthalmia, where the inflammation is more diffuse, involving all layers

q: Where is the likely lesion if patient cannot see right visual field images from both eyes?
e:
B. Left Optic tract
Explanation
The lesion in the left optic tract will cause loss of the right visual field in both eyes due to the crossed nature of visual information. The optic tract transmits visual information from the opposite visual field, so the left tract affects the right visual field of both eyes

Other options:
A) Left Occipital Lobe: A lesion in the left occipital lobe would affect the visual field in the right side, but it would cause homonymous hemianopia (loss of right visual field in both eyes), not specifically from the right visual field from both eyes. Visual fields are processed in the occipital cortex, but this would affect a larger area, including both eyes, in the same visual field
C) Optic Chiasma: A lesion at the optic chiasma typically affects the nasal fibers from both optic nerves, resulting in bitemporal hemianopia (loss of vision from the outer half of both eyes), not the right visual field of both eyes
D) Right Optic Nerve: A lesion in the right optic nerve would affect vision in the right eye and cause monocular blindness in that eye, but not a loss of the right visual field in both eyes

q: A person has chisel injury while stone cutting. Which investigation is detrimental to diagnose?
e:
B. MRI
Explanation
MRI is not ideal in cases involving metallic foreign bodies, as the strong magnetic field can cause the foreign object to move, potentially worsening the injury. In the case of a stone-cutting injury, there might be a metallic foreign body involved, and MRI could pose significant risks. MRI is best suited for soft tissue injuries but should be avoided when metal foreign bodies are suspected due to the potential for dangerous interactions with the magnetic field A) X-ray Orbit: X-ray is generally useful for detecting fractures of the bony orbit but not the best option for assessing soft tissue damage or foreign bodies in the eye or orbit. However, in certain cases, X-ray can provide initial screening to identify bone fractures or if a radiopaque foreign body is suspected C) CT orbit is the gold standard for evaluating orbital injuries, particularly if there is a concern about fractures of the orbital bones, foreign body localization, and soft tissue injuries. CT is also ideal for detecting radiopaque foreign bodies and assessing the extent of the injury in detail D) USG B-scan: USG B-scan is useful for evaluating the posterior segment of the eye, particularly in cases where there is retinal detachment, vitreous hemorrhage, or foreign bodies. However, it would not be as useful as CT for a detailed evaluation of orbital fractures or for detecting radiopaque foreign bodies

q: Most common complication of the following pic?
e:
A. Exposure keratopathy
Explanation
A coloboma is a congenital condition characterized by a defect or gap in the structure of the eye, often in the iris, retina, or optic disc. It results from an incomplete closure of the fetal fissure during eye development. The most common complication associated with coloboma is exposure keratopathy, especially when the coloboma involves the iris or lids

Other options:
B) Cataracts can be a potential complication in individuals with coloboma, especially if the lens is affected. However, cataract is not the most common complication compared to exposure keratopathy, which is more directly related to the eyelid and corneal protection
C) Amblyopia can occur in cases of visual impairment due to coloboma, especially if the condition leads to significant visual defects or misalignment. However, it is less common than exposure keratopathy and typically results from abnormal vision development, which may not always be associated with coloboma
D) Restricted Movements are generally associated with ocular motility disorders and are not a common complication of coloboma. Coloboma typically does not restrict the movement of the eyeball; it primarily affects the anatomical structure of the eye

q: Which glycosaminoglycan maintains corneal transparency?
e:
B. Keratan sulfate
Explanation
Keratan sulfate is the primary glycosaminoglycan (GAG) responsible for maintaining corneal transparency. It is found in the corneal stroma and helps to regulate collagen fibril spacing and hydration, ensuring light transmission without scattering Other Options: A) Heparan sulfate: Found in basement membranes and plays a role in cell signaling and vascular permeability, but it is not primarily involved in corneal transparency C) Hyaluronic acid: Found in the vitreous humor of the eye and is involved in joint lubrication and wound healing, but it does not contribute significantly to corneal transparency D) Chondroitin sulfate: Present in cartilage and connective tissue, providing structural support, but it does not play a major role in maintaining corneal transparency

q: 15 year oldchild came with recent non acceptance of regular glasses for myopic astigmatism. What will be viable option?
e:
A. Spherical equivalent spectacles
Explanation
In a 15-year-old child, LASIK, FemtoLASIK, and Implantable Collamer Lenses (ICL) are not viable options because refractive surgery is contraindicated in individuals under 18 years due to unstable refractive error. Spherical Equivalent Spectacles are the best choice when a patient does not accept their regular cylindrical correction for myopic astigmatism. This method involves averaging the spherical and cylindrical powers to reduce distortion and improve tolerance

Other options:
B) LASIK: Contraindicated in patients under 18 years as their refractive error is still changing.
C) Femto LASIK: Similar to LASIK but uses a femtosecond laser for flap creation and not recommended for minors due to progressive myopia
D) Implantable Collamer Lens (ICL): Used for high myopia but not recommended until refractive stability is confirmed, typically after 21 years of age

q: The given sign is probably seen in which of the folowing?
o: Dot and blot hemorrhages, Diabetes mellitus
e:
A. Hard exudates, Diabetismellitus
Explanation
Hard exudates are lipid and protein deposits from leaking capillaries, commonly seen in diabetic retinopathy

Other options:
B) Soft exudates, Hypertension: Soft exudates (cotton wool spots) indicate retinal ischemia and are seen in hypertensive retinopathy and diabetes
C) Flame-shaped hemorrhages, Hypertension: Flame hemorrhages result from ruptured superficial retinal capillaries, commonly associated with hypertension
D) Dot and blot hemorrhages, Diabetes mellitus: These deeper retinal hemorrhages occur due to microaneurysms and capillary leakage in diabetic retinopathy

q: A new bornchild with big blue eyes and watering. What will be the probable diagnosis?
e:
A. Congenital glaucoma
Explanation
Congenital glaucoma is characterized by buphthalmos (enlarged eyes), corneal edema, excessive tearing, and photophobia due to increased intraocular pressure (IOP). The condition is caused by a developmental defect in the trabecular meshwork, leading to impaired aqueous humour drainage

Other options:
B) Mucopolysaccharidosis: This is a lysosomal storage disorder leading to corneal clouding, skeletal abnormalities, and mental retardation. It does not present with big blue eyes and excessive watering
C) Cataract: Congenital cataract presents as lens opacification and leukocoria (white reflex in the eye), but it does not cause enlarged blue eyes or excessive tearing
D) Ophthalmia neonatorum: A neonatal conjunctivitis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, or other infections, presenting with purulent discharge and swollen eyelids rather than big blue eyes and tearing

q: A patient with history of contact lens use for 2 years now presents with irritation in eyes and sign as in pic. What is most probable diagnosis?
e:
A. Giant papillary conjunctivitis
Explanation
Giant Papillary Conjunctivitis (GPC) is common in contact lens wearers, prosthetic eye users, or those with ocular sutures. It is characterized by large cobblestone papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva, itching, discomfort, excessive mucus discharge, and intolerance to contact lenses and caused by a hypersensitivity reaction to mechanical irritation and protein deposits on contact lenses

Other options:
B) Follicular Conjunctivitis is characterized by small dome-shaped follicles on the conjunctiva, commonly due to viral infections (adenovirus), chlamydia, or chronic allergic reactions
C) Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) is common in young males with seasonal allergic conjunctivitis, especially in warm climates. Giant cobblestone papillae are seen but associated with intense itching, ropy discharge, and photophobia
D) Trachoma is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis (serotypes A-C). It presents with follicular conjunctivitis, pannus formation (corneal neovascularization), and Herbert’s pits

q: History of dryness, corneal softening, night blindness & gritty sensation. The above symptoms due to which vitamin deficiency?
e:
D. Retinoic acid
Explanation
Retinoic acid (Vitamin A) deficiency is associated with dryness of the conjunctiva (xerophthalmia), corneal softening (keratomalacia), and night blindness (nyctalopia). Vitamin A is crucial for the health of the corneal epithelium and the function of rods in the retina, which are responsible for vision in low light

Other options:
A) Iron: Iron deficiency primarily affects hemoglobin production and can lead to anemia, not symptoms like dryness, corneal softening, or night blindness
B) Protein: Protein deficiency can lead to general malnutrition, growth retardation, and other systemic symptoms but is not specifically associated with eye dryness, corneal softening, or night blindness
C) Niacin: Niacin deficiency causes pellagra, characterized by diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia. It doesn't lead to eye dryness, corneal softening, or night blindness

q: A child presented with U/L white pupillary reflex for which surgery was done. Biopsy of the surgical specimen showed flexnerwintersteinerrosette. What is the possible diagnosis?
e:
A. Retinoblastoma
Explanation
Retinoblastoma is a malignant tumor of the retina and the most common cause of white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) in children. Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes are a histopathological feature of retinoblastoma, characterized by tumor cells arranged in a rosette-like pattern around a central lumen, resembling the normal structure of the retina

Other options:
B) Medulloblastoma is a malignant brain tumor typically found in the posterior fossa. It does not cause white pupillary reflex or show Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes in its histology
C) Rhabdomyosarcoma is a soft tissue tumor, usually involving muscle tissue, and it does not exhibit Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes or cause a white pupillary reflex in children
D) Astrocytoma is a glial cell tumor and is typically found in the brain or spinal cord. It does not present with white pupillary reflex or Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes

q: Drug of choice for a patient of glaucoma with brochialasthma?
e:
B. Latanoprost
Explanation
Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analogue used to treat glaucoma by lowering intraocular pressure (IOP). It is preferred in patients with bronchial asthma because it has minimal broncho-constrictive effects compared to other prostaglandin analogues and is safer for use in asthmatic individuals

Other options:
A) Gemoprost is a prostaglandin analog used for inducing abortion or for the treatment of intraocular pressure (IOP) but is not typically used in glaucoma with asthma patients due to its potential for causing bronchoconstriction
C) Carboprost is a prostaglandin analog used for inducing abortion and for controlling postpartum hemorrhage. It can induce bronchospasm and should be avoided in asthma patients
D) Alprostadil is used for erectile dysfunction and in neonatal ductus arteriosus closure, not for glaucoma management. It has vasodilatory effects but is not indicated for glaucoma, especially in asthma patients

q: Most characteristic sign of fungal keratitis
e:
B. Satellite lesions
Explanation
Satellite lesions are characteristic of fungal keratitis, where small, round lesions form around the central corneal infection

Other options:
A) Dendrite: Dendritic ulcers are typically seen in herpes simplex keratitis, not fungal keratitis. It presents as a branching pattern on the cornea
C) White hypopyon (a white layer of pus in the anterior chamber) can be seen in various infections, including bacterial keratitis and fungal keratitis, but it is not the most characteristic sign of fungal keratitis
D) Ring abscess seen in acanthamoeba keratitis

q: Which vitamin in high doses causes macular edema and macular cyst?
e:
D. Niacin
Explanation
Niacin (Vitamin B3), when taken in high doses, is known to cause side effects like flushing, but it is also associated with macular edema and macular cysts, particularly in individuals receiving high doses for hyperlipidemia treatment. This can affect the retina and cause vision problems

Other options:
A) Vitamin A: High doses of vitamin A can cause toxicity and symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and blurry vision, but it is not typically associated with macular edema or macular cysts
B) Vitamin D: Excessive vitamin D can lead to hypercalcemia, but it is not linked to macular edema or cyst formation in the eye
C) Vitamin E: Vitamin E toxicity can cause symptoms like gastrointestinal discomfort and bleeding, but it does not cause macular edema or cysts

q: Pre-requisite for sympathetic ophthalmitis:
e:
A. Penetrating trauma to eye
Explanation
Sympathetic ophthalmia is a bilateral granulomatous uveitis that occurs after penetrating trauma or intraocular surgery, due to an autoimmune response against exposed ocular antigens

Other options:
B) Blunt ocular trauma: While blunt trauma can cause severe eye injuries, it does not typically expose intraocular antigens in a way that triggers sympathetic ophthalmia
C) Chemical injury: Chemical burns primarily cause direct toxicity and inflammation but do not involve the immune-mediated response characteristic of sympathetic ophthalmia
D) UTI: Urinary tract infections have no direct connection with sympathetic ophthalmia, which is an ocular immune response triggered by penetrating trauma

q: Which layer of cornea helps in maintaining hydration of stroma of cornea?
e:
B. Endothelium
Explanation
The corneal endothelium contains Na?/K? ATPase pumps that actively pump excess fluid out of the stroma, maintaining corneal clarity and hydration.

Other options:
A) Descemet’s membrane: This is a basement membrane for the corneal endothelium but does not play a direct role in fluid regulation
C) Epithelium: acts as a barrier to prevent excessive tear film absorption, it does not primarily regulate stromal hydration
D) Stroma: The stroma consists of collagen and glycosaminoglycans that retain water, but it relies on the endothelium to prevent excessive hydration and maintain transparency.

q: Extra set of eyelashes coming from posterior aspect of eyelid margin is known as
e:
A. Distichiasis
Explanation
Extra set row of eye lash due to metaplasia of mebobian glands into eye lashes this is known as distichiasis

q: A patient has u/l proptosis with b/l6th nerve palsy. What could be the possible cause?
e:
A. Cavernous sinus thrombosis
Explanation
Cavernous sinus thrombosis: Causes bilateral cranial nerve palsies (commonly affecting CN VI first) and unilateral proptosis due to venous congestion. It results from infections spreading from the face

Other options:
B) Thyroid ophthalmopathy: Typically causes bilateral proptosis and does not cause cranial nerve palsies in early stages
C) Retinoblastoma: Primarily affects children and presents with leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) and sometimes proptosis, but does not cause bilateral CN VI palsy
D) Orbital pseudotumor: Causes painful proptosis but is typically unilateral and does not lead to bilateral CN VI palsy

q: Shifting fluid sign is seen in
e:
C. Exudative
Explanation
Exudative retinal detachment is characterized by fluid accumulation beneath the retina without retinal tears or breaks. The fluid accumulation can shift when the patient changes position, producing a shifting fluid sign

Other options:
A) Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment is caused by a retinal tear or break, leading to fluid accumulation under the retina but does not specifically cause a shifting fluid sign
B) Tractional retinal detachment occurs when fibrous tissue contracts on the retina, pulling it away. It is not typically associated with a shifting fluid sign
D) Retinal dialysis is a type of retinal tear that typically does not cause the shifting fluid sign but can lead to retinal detachment

q: Esotropia is most commonly associatedwith:
e:
A. Hyperopia
Explanation
Esotropia (inward turning of the eye) is most commonly associated with hyperopia (farsightedness). In hyperopia, the eye tends to focus behind the retina, causing the eye to converge (turn inward) to compensate for the blurred vision, often leading to esotropia

Other options:
B) Myopia is typically associated with exotropia (outward turning of the eye), not esotropia
C) Presbyopia is the age-related loss of accommodation and is not directly linked to esotropia
D) Astigmatism can cause visual disturbances, it is not directly linked to esotropia

q: Incongruous with Wernekieshemianopicpupil is seen in lesion of?
e:
A. Optic tract
Explanation
The incongruous Wernicke's hemianopic pupil is associated with a lesion in the optic tract. A lesion here causes a visual field defect that is not symmetrical (incongruous) in both eyes, as well as abnormal pupillary light reflexes (the Wernicke hemianopic pupil)

Other options:
B) Visual cortex: A lesion in the visual cortex can result in homonymous hemianopia but does not specifically lead to Wernicke's hemianopic pupil. The visual cortex processes visual information, and a lesion here can cause a visual field loss without direct effect on pupillary reflexes
C) Optic radiation: Lesions in the optic radiation can also cause homonymous visual field defects, but the Wernicke's hemianopic pupil is more specifically linked to optic tract lesions
D) Optic nerve: Damage to the optic nerve typically causes monocular visual field loss, not the incongruous visual field defect seen in Wernicke's hemianopic pupil

q: A 65yrs old male with his of Diabetes and Hypertension presents to OPD with complaints of diplopia and squint. On examination secondary deviation is seen to be more than primary deviation. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis:
e:
A. Paralytic squint
Explanation
In paralytic squint, one of the eye muscles is paralyzed, causing misalignment of the eyes. This results in a secondary deviation (the eye with the weaker muscle) being more pronounced than the primary deviation (the unaffected eye). Diplopia (double vision) is a common symptom in paralytic squint

Other options:
B) Incomitant squint can occur due to a variety of causes, including paralytic or restrictive causes, but it doesn’t typically describe the relationship between primary and secondary deviation. The secondary deviation being more pronounced is characteristic of paralytic squint
C) Restrictive squint occurs due to physical restrictions (e.g., fibrosis or scarring of the muscles), limiting eye movement. While secondary deviation can also be more pronounced in restrictive squint, the most likely cause in this scenario with diabetes and hypertension is paralytic squint due to nerve involvement
D) Pseudo squint refers to an apparent squint, often due to anatomical features like epicanthal folds or a wide nasal bridge. It doesn’t cause actual misalignment or diplopia, so the secondary deviation would not be more than the primary deviation

q: In which nerve palsy, this action wound’tbe possible?
e:
A. 3rd
Explanation
The third cranial nerve (oculomotor nerve) innervates the superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, and inferior oblique muscles. Levo-elevation requires superior rectus and inferior oblique to function properly. In oculomotor nerve palsy, both these muscles are affected, making this movement impossible

Other options:
B) 4th nerve palsy (Trochlear nerve palsy): Affects superior oblique, leading to vertical diplopia, but does not affect levo-elevation
C) 6th nerve palsy (Abducens nerve palsy): Affects lateral rectus, causing difficulty in abduction but not in elevation
D) 7th nerve palsy (Facial nerve palsy): Affects facial muscles, not extraocular muscles

q: Middle aged women with B/L proptosis, with restricted ocular movements and chemosis, is eurothyroid. What is probable diagnosis?
e:
A. Thyroid ophthalmopathy
Explanation
Thyroid ophthalmopathy: Most commonly seen in Graves' disease, with euthyroid or hyperthyroid status, but typically has painless bilateral proptosis and specific extraocular muscle involvement (muscle belly enlargement sparing the tendon)

Other options:
B) Orbital pseudotumor usually affects the tendon also
C) Orbital cellulitis: Usually unilateral, presents with fever, acute onset, pain, and systemic signs of infection (e.g., sinusitis)
D) Orbital lymphoma: Causes painless, slow-growing proptosis without inflammation, chemosis, or restricted movements

q: Photostresstest is used to differentiate
e:
A. Optic nerve and macular function
Explanation
The photostress test is used to differentiate between macular disease and optic nerve disease by assessing the recovery time after exposure to bright light

Other options:
B) Retina and vitreous: The test does not differentiate between retinal and vitreous disorders
C) Cataract and glaucoma: Cataracts affect lens opacity, and glaucoma is a disease of optic nerve damage; this test does not help differentiate them
D) Cornea and lens lesions: Corneal and lens disorders affect refraction and transparency but are not evaluated by this test

q: Drug decreasdIOP possibly by act on uveoscleral outflow
e:
A. Latanoprost
Explanation
Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analog that primarily works by increasing the uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humor, which helps reduce intraocular pressure (IOP). It is one of the most commonly prescribed medications for glaucoma

Other options:
B) Timolol: Timolol is a beta-blocker that reduces IOP primarily by decreasing aqueous humor production, not by affecting uveoscleral outflow
C) Pilocarpine: Pilocarpine is a miotic agent that works by increasing trabecular outflow, not uveoscleral outflow
D) Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors: These drugs reduce IOP by decreasing aqueous humor production, not by affecting outflow pathways

q: A patient of chronic arthritis taking a drug developed difficulty in vision. On examination , no bulls eye findings of fundus observed. But later it was noticed that he was developing corneal pathology. What is the appropriate drug?
e:
D. Chloroquine
Explanation
Chloroquine is an antimalarial drug often used to treat systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumatoid arthritis. One of the well-known side effects of chloroquine is corneal toxicity, which can lead to vision changes. This toxicity typically manifests as a corneal deposit or corneal pathology, which might not always present with the classic "bull's eye" maculopathy seen in other conditions, like hydroxychloroquine toxicity

Other options:
A) Sulfasalazine can cause some ocular side effects, such as dry eye or conjunctivitis, corneal pathology is not a typical side effect
B) Leflunomide used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, is associated with liver toxicity and teratogenicity, but not with corneal toxicity
C) Methotrexate can cause ocular toxicity (such as dry eye or retinal changes), but corneal pathology is not a common complication

q: Identify the given instrument
e:
A. Maddox rod
Explanation
Maddox rod is an optical instrument used in ophthalmology to assess heterophoria or ocular alignment. It is typically used during a cover test to detect and measure strabismus or misalignment of the eyes. The rod consists of a series of parallel red or white cylindrical lenses, and it helps in detecting binocular vision issues by splitting the light entering the eye, creating a visual illusion that allows the examiner to assess eye movement and alignment.

Other options:
B) Maddox wing: This is another device used for measuring ocular alignment and detecting binocular vision problems, but it is a different method than the Maddox rod
C) Maddox glass: This term isn't commonly used to describe an established instrument in clinical practice
D) Red glasses: Red glasses are typically used for color vision testing or testing depth perception, not for assessing ocular alignment

q: Identify the test as shown in the image
e:
A. Cover uncover test
Explanation
The cover-uncover test is a clinical procedure used to detect heterophoria or strabismus (misalignment of the eyes). The test is typically performed by covering one eye while the patient focuses on a target. After uncovering the eye, the examiner observes any movement in the uncovered eye to detect misalignment. This test helps identify issues such as tropia (constant misalignment) or phoria (latent misalignment)

Other options:
B) Prism bar tests: These tests are used to measure the degree of ocular misalignment (strabismus) by placing different prisms in front of the eyes
C) Pin hole test: This test is used to assess refractive error and determine if vision problems are due to refractive issues, such as nearsightedness or farsightedness

q: Chemotherapy agents for retinoblastoma are
e:
A. Vincristine, carboplatin, etopside
Explanation
The standard chemotherapy regimen for retinoblastoma includes a combination of • Vincristine (a microtubule inhibitor) • Carboplatin (a platinum-based alkylating agent) • Etoposide (a topoisomerase II inhibitor)

Other options:
B) Vinblastine, Etoposide, Bleomycin: This is more commonly used in Hodgkin's lymphoma, not retinoblastoma
C) Vincristine, Vinblastine, Etoposide: Vinblastine is not typically used for retinoblastoma treatment
D) Vincristine, Vinblastine, Cisplatin: Cisplatin is more common in germ cell tumors, and Vinblastine is not part of the standard retinoblastoma regimen

q: Seton surgery is
e:
A. Drainage implant
Explanation
Seton surgery refers to the use of a glaucoma drainage device (GDD) to facilitate aqueous humor drainage from the anterior chamber to an external reservoir, thereby lowering intraocular pressure (IOP). It is commonly used in refractory glaucoma cases where trabeculectomy has failed or is not suitable

Other options:
B) Trabeculectomy: A filtering surgery where a drainage fistula is created to allow aqueous humor to flow from the anterior chamber to the subconjunctival space. It does not involve an implant
C) Trabeculotomy: A procedure that involves cutting the trabecular meshwork to improve aqueous outflow, commonly used in congenital glaucoma
D) Goniotomy: A surgical procedure in congenital glaucoma where the trabecular meshwork is incised under gonioscopic guidance to enhance drainage

q: Which is the most common ocular finding in myasthenia gravis
e:
A. Ptosis
Explanation
Ptosis (drooping of the eyelid) is the most common ocular finding in myasthenia gravis (MG). It occurs due to weakness of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle, which is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (CN III). The ptosis in MG is typically variable and worsens with fatigue

Other options:
B) Lagophthalmos: Incomplete eyelid closure, usually seen in facial nerve palsy rather than MG
C) Proptosis: Forward protrusion of the eye, commonly seen in thyroid eye disease, not MG
D) Enophthalmos: Posterior displacement of the eye, seen in Horner's syndrome or orbital trauma, not MG

q: Which of the following is decreased in retinitis pigmentosa?
e:
D. Docosahexanoic acid
Explanation
Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a group of inherited retinal degenerative diseases characterized by progressive photoreceptor loss (primarily rods, followed by cones). Studies have shown that Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), an omega-3 fatty acid essential for retinal function, is significantly decreased in RP

Other options:
A) Arachidonic acid: A polyunsaturated fatty acid involved in inflammation but not primarily affected in RP
B) Treilonic acid: This is not a recognized fatty acid
C) Thromboxane: A lipid mediator involved in platelet aggregation and hemostasis, not directly related to RP

q: Which of the following is against the rule correction astigmatism?
e:
A. -1.25 Cyl90
Explanation
Astigmatism is classified based on the orientation of the steepest corneal meridian • With-the-rule (WTR) astigmatism: Steepest meridian at 90° (vertical axis) ? Corrected with negative cylinder at 180° • Against-the-rule (ATR) astigmatism: Steepest meridian at 180° (horizontal axis) ? Corrected with negative cylinder at 90° -1.25 cyl 90°: This applies a negative cylinder at 90°, which is used to correct against-the-rule (ATR) astigmatism

Other options:
B) -2 spherical: Spherical correction applies equally in all meridians, not specific to astigmatism
C) -3 cyl 180°: This applies a negative cylinder at 180°, which corrects with-the-rule (WTR) astigmatism
D) +2 cyl 90°: This is a plus cylinder prescription, which is used in some cases but does not fit the standard rule-based correction

q: A child has ptosis and poor levatorfunction. What is the surgery of choice?
e:
D. Fascia latasling
Explanation
Ptosis with poor levator function (<4 mm) requires a frontalis suspension (fascia lata sling) procedure because the levator muscle is too weak to be effectively tightened or resected. Instead, the frontalis muscle is used to elevate the eyelid through a sling mechanism

Other options:
Levator muscle resection (Option
A) is preferred for ptosis with moderate to good levator function Mullerectomy (Option
B) and Fasanella-Servat procedure (Option
C) are typically used for mild ptosis with good levator function and a good response to phenylephrine testing

q: Mannitol is not given in which situation
e:
A. Pulmonary edema
Explanation
Mannitol is contraindicated in pulmonary edema because it is an osmotic diuretic that initially increases intravascular volume, which can worsen pulmonary congestion and fluid overload

Other options:
It is used in high intracranial hypertension (B) and cerebral edema (D) to reduce brain swelling by drawing fluid out of brain tissue into the bloodstream In drug poisoning (C), mannitol can be used to enhance renal excretion of toxins by inducing diuresis

q: Which glaucoma drug is not given in children with sleep apnea
e:
B. Brimonidine
Explanation
Brimonidine (?2-adrenergic agonist) is contraindicated in children, especially those under 2 years of age, due to the risk of central nervous system (CNS) depression, lethargy, apnea, and even respiratory arrest

Other options:
Mannitol (A) is an osmotic diuretic used in acute angle-closure glaucoma but does not affect sleep apnea Pilocarpine (C) is a miotic agent that has no significant effect on respiration Acetazolamide (D) is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and does not have CNS depressant effects that would worsen sleep apnea

q: True statement about given condition of eye are all except
o: Decreased vision is due to astigmatism
Surgery is the treatment of choice
Infrared raysexposure is a risk factor
e:
D. Infrared raysexposure is a risk factor
Explanation
Option D (infrared rays exposure as a risk factor) ? false as UV radiation (especially UV-B) is the primary risk factor, not infrared rays. Pterygium is more common in individuals with prolonged sun exposure

Other options:
Option A (mostly arise from nasal conjunctiva) ? true Option B (decreased vision due to astigmatism) ? true because the irregular surface of the pterygium induces astigmatism, leading to vision impairment Option C (surgery is the treatment of choice) ? true but only for cases with significant visual impairment or cosmetic concerns

q: Most common cause of fungal orbital cellulitis in patient of diabetic ketoacidosis is?
e:
B. Mucor
Explanation
Mucormycosis (caused by Mucor species) is the most common cause of fungal orbital cellulitis in patients with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). It is an opportunistic fungal infection that spreads rapidly through the sinuses into the orbit and brain, leading to rhinocerebral mucormycosis

Other options:
Aspergillus (A) is more commonly associated with chronic invasive sinusitis in immunocompromised patients but is not the most common cause in DKA Candida (C) usually causes systemic candidiasis and does not commonly present as orbital cellulitis Cryptococcus (D) is more associated with meningitis in immunocompromised individuals (e.g., HIV/AIDS)

q: Most common orbital wall fractured in blow out fracture orbit is?
e:
C. Floor
Explanation
The floor of the orbit is the most common site of fracture in blow-out fractures of the orbit Blow-out fractures typically occur when an object strikes the globe (eyeball), causing increased intraorbital pressure, which leads to a fracture of the thin walls of the orbit. The floor of the orbit is particularly susceptible because it is the thinnest of the orbital walls, and the forces from blunt trauma often cause the orbital contents (such as the inferior rectus) to push against it, leading to a "trapdoor" fracture

Other options:
Medial wall (A) is also commonly involved in orbital fractures, especially in cases of nasal trauma Lateral wall (B) and roof (D) fractures are less common in blow-out fractures compared to the floor

q: What is the yoke muscle of right eye lateral rectus in dextroversion?
e:
A. Medial rectus left eye
Explanation
In dextroversion (rightward gaze), the lateral rectus of the right eye contracts to move the eye to the right. The medial rectus of the left eye is the corresponding yoke muscle that works synergistically with the right eye's lateral rectus. This coordinated action allows for both eyes to move in the same direction Yoke muscles: In conjugate gaze (both eyes moving in the same direction), the yoke muscles are the muscles of the opposite eye that work together to produce coordinated eye movement For dextroversion, the lateral rectus of the right eye and medial rectus of the left eye are the yoke muscles In levoversion (leftward gaze), the medial rectus of the right eye and lateral rectus of the left eye are the corresponding yoke muscles

q: 100 dayglaucoma is caused due to?
e:
A. Central retinal vein occlusion
Explanation
100-day glaucoma refers to a form of secondary glaucoma that can occur after central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). It typically develops 2-4 months after CRVO, hence the term "100-day glaucoma." The condition is caused by neovascularization of the iris and anterior chamber angle, leading to elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) Other Options: B) Photolysis refers to the breakdown of a cataract and is typically not associated with secondary glaucoma in the way CRVO is C) Neovascularization in diabetes can lead to diabetic retinopathy and is a potential cause of neovascular glaucoma, but it is not referred to as 100-day glaucoma D) RD (Retinal Detachment) is not typically associated with 100-day glaucoma, though it may lead to other forms of ocular complications

q: A diabetic patient came two days after cataract surgery with following presentation. He also has severe pain and redness in eyes. Which of the following is the first step in the management of this patient?
e:
A. Intravitreal antibiotic
Explanation
Given that the patient presents with severe pain, redness, and a history of recent cataract surgery, the most likely diagnosis is endophthalmitis, which is an infection inside the eye that can occur postoperatively. Endophthalmitis is a medical emergency and can lead to rapid vision loss if not treated promptly The first step in managing endophthalmitis is intravitreal antibiotics to control the infection and prevent further complications, such as vision loss. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are typically used for this purpose Other Options: B) Intravitreal steroids: These are generally used to reduce inflammation but are not effective in treating infection. In the presence of infection, steroids can worsen the condition C) Intravenous mannitol: Mannitol is used in cases of acute glaucoma or elevated intraocular pressure, not for treating infections like endophthalmitis D) Intravenous antibiotics: While systemic antibiotics may be used in some cases, intravitreal antibiotics are the mainstay of treatment for intraocular infections like endophthalmitis

q: Third nerve palsy in diabetes mellitus presents with?
e:
D. Normal pupillary reflex
Explanation
In diabetic third nerve palsy, the most common presentation includes ptosis and ocular motility restriction, specifically in the movements of the affected eye. However, one of the key features of third nerve palsy in the context of diabetes is that it often spares the pupillary reflex. This is due to the fact that the fibers controlling the pupil (which are located on the outer aspect of the third cranial nerve) are often not involved in diabetic ischemic neuropathy. Therefore, pupillary reflex remains normal in many diabetic third nerve palsy cases Other Options: A) Pseudoptosis: This can occur in cases of diabetic third nerve palsy due to the weakness of the levator palpebrae muscle, but true ptosis is more commonly observed B) Proptosis: Proptosis (bulging of the eye) is typically associated with conditions such as thyroid eye disease or orbital tumors, not third nerve palsy C) Abnormal pupillary reflex: This would be more likely in compressive third nerve palsy (e.g., caused by an aneurysm or tumor), but in diabetic third nerve palsy, the pupillary reflex is usually spared

q: A 50-years-old patient presented with a history of STD and came to OPD with neurological abnormality. Which of the following is true?
o: Normal light reflex, accommodation reflex lost
Absent light reflex, accommodation reflex normal
e:
B. Absent light reflex, accommodation reflex normal
Explanation
The condition described seems to suggest neurosyphilis, particularly tabes dorsalis or general paresis of the insane. Neurosyphilis can cause a variety of neurological deficits, and one classic finding is Argyll Robertson pupils, which are small, irregular pupils that react abnormally to light but accommodate normally. This means that the light reflex is lost, but the accommodation reflex remains intact. Other Options: A) Normal light reflex and accommodation reflex lost: This is not typical for neurosyphilis or any related condition as in this case, the light reflex is typically absent but accommodation remains normal C) Both lost: Both light and accommodation reflexes would be lost in conditions affecting the parasympathetic pathway, such as in severe optic or oculomotor nerve lesions, not typical in neurosyphilis D) Both normal: This would be inconsistent with the findings in neurosyphilis, where light reflex abnormalities are characteristic

q: A surgeon was doing strabismus surgery on a child, when there was a severe decrease in heart rate, what immediate step you will take to manage?
e:
C. Stop surgery immediately
Explanation
A severe decrease in heart rate (bradycardia) during strabismus surgery could indicate a vagal response due to ocular manipulation, which is known to cause significant vagal stimulation, leading to bradycardia. In this situation, the immediate step would be to stop the surgery to avoid further vagal stimulation, assess the patient's condition, and provide appropriate resuscitation if necessary Other Options: A) Lessen the plane of anesthesia: While reducing anesthetic depth can sometimes help in managing bradycardia, the first step should be stopping the surgery to prevent further vagal stimulation B) Atropine: Atropine is often used to treat bradycardia, but the immediate first step is stopping the surgery and assessing the situation. Atropine can be administered if bradycardia persists, but it's not the first immediate action in this scenario D) Glycopyrrolate: Glycopyrrolate, like atropine, can be used to treat bradycardia, but the first immediate action should be halting the surgery to prevent further vagal stimulus

q: Which conjunctivitis results in blindness in neonates?
e:
C. Neisseria
Explanation
Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a serious cause of conjunctivitis in neonates, also known as gonococcal conjunctivitis. If left untreated, it can lead to severe complications, including corneal ulceration and permanent blindness. Neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis is typically acquired during delivery from an infected mother Other Options: A) Chemical conjunctivitis: While common in neonates due to exposure to chemicals (e.g., silver nitrate used as a prophylactic agent), it does not typically lead to blindness and usually resolves with appropriate care B) Chlamydia: Chlamydial conjunctivitis can cause significant damage to the eyes and can lead to scarring and possible vision impairment if not treated, but it is less likely to cause immediate blindness compared to gonococcal infection D) Adenovirus: This can cause viral conjunctivitis, but it is not a major cause of blindness in neonates. Adenoviral conjunctivitis is usually self-limiting and does not result in permanent vision loss

q: Which of the following enterovirus causes hemorrhagic conjunctivitis?
e:
A. E70
Explanation
Enterovirus 70 (EV70) is a well-known cause of acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis (AHC), a highly contagious viral eye infection characterized by sudden onset of subconjunctival hemorrhage, pain, photophobia, and watery discharge. It spreads rapidly through direct contact and contaminated surfaces Other Options: B) E72, C) E69 – These are not known to cause hemorrhagic conjunctivitis D) E71 (Enterovirus 71) – While EV71 is associated with hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) and neurological complications, it is not a primary cause of hemorrhagic conjunctivitis

q: Which neonatal conjunctivitis is most severe?
e:
A. Neisseria
Explanation
Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the most severe form. It presents within 2-5 days of birth with profuse purulent discharge, severe eyelid edema, and corneal ulceration, which can rapidly progress to perforation and blindness if untreated. It requires urgent treatment with systemic and topical antibiotics (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime) Other Options: B) Chlamydia – More common but less severe than gonococcal conjunctivitis. Presents with mucopurulent discharge, but rarely leads to blindness C) Adenovirus – Causes a mild viral conjunctivitis that is self-limiting D) Chemical conjunctivitis – Caused by silver nitrate drops used for prophylaxis, presenting within 24 hours with mild redness and watery discharge, but resolves quickly without complications

q: Which of the following is an example of simple myopic astigmatism?
o: -2 D spherical and +1 cylindrical at 90 degree
e:
A. -2 D cylindrical at 90 degrees
Explanation
Simple Myopic Astigmatism occurs when one meridian is myopic while the other is emmetropic (i.e., one focus falls on the retina while the other falls in front of it) Option A (-2 D cylindrical at 90°): This indicates that one meridian has -2 D of myopia, while the perpendicular meridian has no refractive error (emmetropic) ? This fits the definition of simple myopic astigmatism Other Options: B (-2 D spherical and +1 cylindrical at 90°): This represents mixed astigmatism because one meridian is myopic (-2 D) and the other is hyperopic C (+2 D spherical and +1 cylindrical at 90°): This represents compound hyperopic astigmatism (both meridians are hyperopic) D (+2 D cylindrical at 180°): This represents simple hyperopic astigmatism (one meridian is hyperopic, and the other is emmetropic)

q: A 25 years old diabetic patient presents with unilateral transient obscuration for 2-3 days followed by sudden diminution of vision. Which of the following test would you order?
e:
A. Serum homocysteine level
Explanation
A 25-year-old diabetic patient presenting with transient obscurations of vision followed by sudden diminution of vision suggests a vascular event, likely retinal vein occlusion (RVO) or ischemic optic neuropathy. Elevated serum homocysteine levels are associated with hypercoagulability, which increases the risk of retinal vascular occlusions in young diabetic patients. Other Options: B) Serum Creatinine Level: Checks for diabetic nephropathy but is not directly related to transient visual loss C) Serum ACE Levels: Elevated in sarcoidosis, which can cause optic neuropathy or uveitis, but does not typically present with transient obscuration of vision D) Quantiferon Gold TB Test: Used for latent tuberculosis, which is not a primary cause of transient vision loss in a diabetic patient

q: Which of the following is true regarding concentration of proteins in senile cataract-
o: More soluble protein, less insoluble protein
More insoluble protein, less soluble protein
Equal concentration of both soluble and insoluble proteins
e:
B. More insoluble protein, less soluble protein
Explanation
In senile cataract, the primary pathological change involves the accumulation of insoluble proteins in the lens fibers, which leads to the clouding of the lens. Over time, the lens proteins undergo aggregation and denaturation, causing a higher concentration of insoluble proteins Other Options: A) More soluble proteins and less insoluble proteins, as senile cataract is characterized by an increase in insoluble proteins, not soluble proteins C) Equal concentration of both soluble and insoluble proteins, as the balance is disturbed in cataracts with more insoluble proteins D) None of the above: Incorrect, as B is the correct answer

q: A 65 year old diabetic woman presents with painless loss of vision. The ocular findings are shown in the image below. What is the likely diagnosis and management for this patient?
o: Immature senile cataract and phacoemulsification with IOL.
e:
D. Immature senile cataract and phacoemulsification with IOL.
Explanation
Immature senile cataract is a common condition in elderly individuals, especially those with diabetes. The patient presents with painless vision loss, which is characteristic of cataracts, particularly when the lens opacity becomes significant. The management for immature senile cataract includes phacoemulsification with intraocular lens (IOL) implantation, which is the standard surgical procedure for cataract removal Other Options: A) Zonular cataract and lensectomy: Zonular cataracts are different from senile cataracts and typically involve the zonules of the lens. Lensectomy is not the first-line treatment, and zonular cataracts may not match this presentation B) Rosette cataract and sugar control: Rosette cataracts are characterized by a particular pattern of opacity that is not typical for diabetic patients with senile cataracts. Sugar control is important for overall health but would not be sufficient as a primary treatment for cataracts C) Sunflower cataract and lesion extraction: Sunflower cataracts are a specific type of cataract associated with Wilson's disease, not typical for diabetic patients. The treatment for these is different and focuses on addressing the underlying condition

q: Which of the following refractive errors is associated with the image given below?
e:
B. Astigmatism
Explanation
Sturm's Conoid refers to the visual pattern created when light rays from a point source focus at different points along two perpendicular meridians due to astigmatism. This occurs because the cornea or lens has an uneven curvature, causing the light entering the eye to focus on multiple points instead of a single point on the retina Astigmatism is the refractive error associated with Sturm's Conoid, where the eye's inability to focus light evenly causes distorted or blurred vision, especially at certain angles Other Options: A) Presbyopia ? Presbyopia is a condition related to age-related changes in the lens, resulting in difficulty focusing on near objects. It does not involve the creation of a conoid pattern and is unrelated to astigmatism C) Hypermetropia (Hyperopia) ? Hypermetropia or farsightedness is when distant objects are focused behind the retina due to the eye being too short or the cornea being too flat. It does not cause the Sturm's Conoid D) Myopia ? Myopia or nearsightedness is when close objects are focused in front of the retina. It is also not associated with the creation of Sturm's Conoid.

q: A 5 year old boy presents with a small nodule on the sclera as shown in the image below. What is the likely diagnosis?
e:
D. Dermoid
Explanation
Dermoid is a benign growth composed of skin-like tissue, including hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and sweat glands. These cysts are commonly located in the limbal area (the junction between the cornea and sclera) and can appear as yellowish, smooth, firm nodules on the sclera Other Options: A) Pterygium is a benign growth of conjunctival tissue that extends over the cornea, typically due to chronic irritation from UV exposure. It is usually triangular in shape, not a small nodule B) Pinguecula is a yellowish, raised lesion on the conjunctiva (usually near the cornea), often caused by UV exposure or aging. It is not typically a nodule on the sclera C) Dermolipoma is a rare, benign congenital lesion composed of adipose tissue, but it is less likely to present as a small nodule on the sclera compared to a dermoid cyst

q: The eye examination of a 20 year old male shows a golden ring on the iris. What is the next investigation to diagnose the condition?
e:
D. Serum ceruloplasmin
Explanation
The golden-brown ring on the iris described in the question is a Kayser-Fleischer (KF) ring, which is a hallmark of Wilson’s disease (hepatolenticular degeneration). Wilson’s disease is a disorder of copper metabolism due to a mutation in the ATP7B gene, leading to copper accumulation in the liver, brain, and cornea. The first-line investigation is serum ceruloplasmin, which is typically low in Wilson’s disease

Other options:
A) Alpha-1 antitrypsin: Used for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, which presents with early-onset COPD and liver disease, not KF rings
B) Alpha-fetoprotein: Marker for hepatocellular carcinoma and germ cell tumors, not Wilson’s disease
C) Serum iron: Relevant for hemochromatosis, which causes bronze skin pigmentation, diabetes, and liver dysfunction, but not KF rings

q: What is the dye and filter used to diagnose corneal ulcers?
o: Fluorescein dye- visualised under green filter
Fluorescein dye- visualised under cobalt light filter
e:
D. Fluorescein dye- visualised under cobalt light filter
Explanation
Viral corneal ulcers, such as herpetic keratitis, are best visualized using fluorescein dye and a cobalt blue filter. Fluorescein dye stains areas of epithelial damage, allowing dendritic or geographic ulcers (caused by HSV) to be identified. Cobalt blue light enhances the fluorescence of the dye, making the ulcer appear bright green Other Options: A) Lissamine dye - Green filter: Lissamine green stains devitalized conjunctival and corneal epithelial cells but is not the primary choice for corneal ulcers B) Lissamine dye - Cobalt blue filter: Lissamine does not fluoresce under cobalt blue light C) Fluorescein dye - Green filter: Green filters enhance contrast but do not cause fluorescence like cobalt blue light does

Other options:
B) Congenital Cataract: Presents as painless leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) but does not cause excessive watering or photophobia
C) Mucopolysaccharidosis: Can cause corneal clouding but is associated with skeletal deformities and developmental delay
D) Ophthalmia Neonatorum: Neonatal conjunctivitis caused by bacterial infections (e.g., gonorrhea or chlamydia) but does not cause photophobia or buphthalmos

q: A 60-year-old patient complains of decreased distant vision but now he does not use spectacles for near vision. What is this type of refractive error called?

Other options:
B) Axial Myopia: Caused by an increase in the length of the eyeball, not lens changes. It is congenital or develops in childhood
C) Curvatural Myopia: Due to an increase in corneal curvature, not due to lens sclerosis
D) Positional Myopia: Caused by a change in lens position, which is rare and does not explain this case

q: Which of the following is not seen in MEN2B?

Explanation

Other options:
A) Marfanoid habitus: Seen in MEN-2B. It refers to a tall, thin body frame with disproportionately long limbs and fingers, resembling Marfan syndrome. This is a characteristic feature of MEN-2B
B) Mucosal neuroma: Seen in MEN-2B. Mucosal neuromas are benign growths of nerve tissue, commonly found in the lips, tongue, and gastrointestinal tract. They are a hallmark of MEN-2B

q: Why does cancer cell undergo Warburg effect?
o: Increase atp production from the pathway.
Useful to make intermediates for survival
To avoid ageing and remain immortal
e:
B. Useful to make intermediates for survival
Explanation
The Warburg effect allows cancer cells to shunt glucose metabolites into biosynthetic pathways. These intermediates are crucial for producing nucleotides, amino acids, and lipids, which are essential for rapid cell growth and survival

Other options:
A) Increase ATP Production from the pathway: The Warburg effect is not primarily about maximizing ATP production. Although aerobic glycolysis is less efficient than oxidative phosphorylation in terms of ATP yield, cancer cells prioritize other benefits from this pathway
C) To avoid aging and remain immortal: Immortality in cancer cells is more closely related to mechanisms like telomerase activation rather than the Warburg effect. The Warburg effect primarily supports anabolic growth rather than directly influencing aging
D) Less glucose uptake by cancer: Cancer cells exhibit increased glucose uptake due to their high metabolic demand, as evidenced by overexpression of glucose transporters (e.g., GLUT1)

q: True about ageing & senescence is?
o: Telomerase activity is increased in ageing
Telomerase and aging are not related
e:
C. Telomerase activity decreases in ageing
Explanation
Telomerase activity is decreased in ageing: In ageing somatic cells, telomerase activity is typically reduced or absent, resulting in telomere shortening. This contributes to cellular senescence and loss of regenerative capacity

Other options:
A) Telomerase activity is increased in ageing: In most somatic cells, telomerase activity decreases with age, leading to telomere shortening, which contributes to cellular senescence and ageing
B) Telomeres increase in ageing: Telomeres progressively shorten with each cell division in somatic cells as organisms age. Shortened telomeres trigger replicative senescence
D) Telomerase and ageing are not related: Telomerase and ageing are closely related, as telomerase helps maintain telomere length and delays cellular senescence in certain cell types, such as germ cells, stem cells, and cancer cells

q: Which of the following mutation will result in the chain termination by introduction of stop codon?
e:
A. Nonsense mutation
Explanation
Nonsense mutation introduces a premature stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA) in the mRNA sequence, leading to the termination of translation and a truncated, often nonfunctional protein

Other options:
B) Missense mutation changes a single nucleotide, resulting in the substitution of one amino acid for another. It does not produce a stop codon
C) Point mutation refers to a change in a single nucleotide, which can result in various outcomes (silent, missense, or nonsense). However, not all point mutations lead to chain termination
D) Silent mutation changes a nucleotide but does not alter the amino acid sequence due to the redundancy of the genetic code

q: Which of the following is AR inheritance?
e:
B. Cystic fibrosis
Explanation
Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene. An individual must inherit two copies of the mutated gene (one from each parent) to develop the disease

Other options:
A) Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the FGFR3 gene. A single copy of the mutated gene is sufficient to cause the condition
C) Treacher Collins syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the TCOF1 gene. Only one copy of the mutated gene is necessary for the condition to manifest
D) Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder, meaning it is primarily seen in males and carried by females. It is not autosomal recessive

q: A 9-year-old child presented with history of recurrent chest infections and abdomen pain and had transfusions in the past. On examination he had splenomegaly, icterus. Investigations shows a peak in S window. Which of the following is correct in the patient?
e:
D. HbSS
Explanation
The patient likely has sickle cell disease, specifically the HbSS variant, where both alleles are mutated to produce sickle haemoglobin (HbS). This explains the recurrent chest infections (possibly due to sickle cell-related lung damage), abdominal pain (often due to splenic infarction or vaso-occlusion), splenomegaly, and icterus (due to hemolysis). The peak in the S window (indicating the presence of HbS) is characteristic of this condition

Other options:
A) Hb A2 is typically elevated in conditions like beta-thalassemia but not in sickle cell disease. This patient's clinical presentation does not suggest a beta-thalassemia diagnosis
B) HbF (fetal haemoglobin) is elevated in conditions like sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia during certain stages, especially in newborns, but this patient's clinical features (recurrent chest infections, splenomegaly, icterus, and transfusions) are more indicative of a sickle cell crisis, not simply an elevated HbF
C) Hb S variant refers to the abnormal haemoglobin seen in sickle cell disease but does not directly correlate with the patient's presentation of recurrent infections, transfusions, and splenomegaly.

q: A woman patient presented to the OPD with a fatigue. Routine CBC analysis showed 9gm % MCV 60 RBC count 5.2 million. Microscopy showed microcyctic RBC's which of the following is the next investigation
e:
B. HBA2
Explanation
The microcytic anemia with a normal RBC count in this patient fits the pattern for thalassemia. Hb A2 is elevated in beta-thalassemia minor, which is a common cause of microcytic anemia. Testing for Hb A2 levels is crucial in confirming this diagnosis

Other options:
A) Ferritin This would be an important test to rule out iron deficiency anemia, but given the RBC count is relatively high (5.2 million), it is less likely to be iron deficiency in this case, and the history or presentation does not strongly suggest it
C) Serum folate levels: Folate deficiency typically leads to macrocytic anemia (high MCV), not microcytic anemia. The patient's microcytic RBCs point to a different etiology, making folate testing less relevant at this stage
D) Homocysteine levels: Elevated homocysteine levels can be associated with folate or vitamin B12 deficiency, which causes macrocytic anemia. This patient's microcytic anemia makes homocysteine testing less appropriate for the initial evaluation

q: A patient presents with haemorrhoids and fatigue. Peripheral smear is as show in the image what is likely diagnosis?
e:
A. Iron deficiency
Explanation
Iron deficiency anemia is the most likely diagnosis. The presence of microcytic hypochromic RBCs and pencil-shaped cells is characteristic of iron deficiency anemia. The fatigue and hemorrhoids are common symptoms, and the peripheral smear findings are typical of iron deficiency anemia, where the body is unable to produce enough hemoglobin due to insufficient iron

Other options:
B) Vitamin B12 deficiency typically leads to macrocytic and megaloblastic RBCs, not microcytic hypochromic cells. Additionally, the presence of pencil-shaped cells is not associated with B12 deficiency
C) Thalassemia can cause microcytic anemia, but the characteristic finding on a peripheral smear would be target cells or basophilic stippling, not pencil-shaped cells. Thalassemia is usually diagnosed with hemoglobin electrophoresis, showing an abnormal pattern of hemoglobin types
D) Sickle cell anemia presents with sickle-shaped cells and nucleated RBCs, which is different from the microcytic hypochromic cells with pencil shapes observed in this patient

q: A 45-year-old male presents with dragging abdomen pain. On examination he was found to have a palpable spleen. Peripheral smear shows - leukocytosis with increase in basophils, myelocytes and metamyelocytes. Which of the following will be seen in the patient?
e:
D. T (9, 22)
Explanation
T (9, 22) translocation is characteristic of Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia (CML), which typically presents with symptoms such as dragging abdominal pain (possibly due to splenomegaly). The peripheral smear in CML often shows leucocytosis with an increase in basophils, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes, which is consistent with the findings described in this patient. The Philadelphia chromosome (t (9, 22)) is a hallmark of CML.

Other options:
A) T (15, 17) This translocation is associated with acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), which is a subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). It is characterized by the presence of promyelocytes and does not typically show leucocytosis with increased basophils, myelocytes, or metamyelocytes, which would be seen in chronic myeloproliferative disorders
B) T (1, 22) This translocation is rarely seen and is associated with lymphoid leukemia in some cases, but it is not a common feature in chronic myeloproliferative diseases or the condition described in the patient
C) T (11, 14) This translocation is associated with mantle cell lymphoma, not with myeloproliferative disorders or the findings in this patient

q: A 10-year-old child with pain the bone and bone showing sclerotic changes. Peripheral smear is as soon MC organism implied in osteomyelitis of the patient is?
e:
C. Salmonella
Explanation
Children with sickle cell disease are at higher risk for osteomyelitis caused by Salmonella species. The sickle-shaped cells in the peripheral smear suggest sickle cell disease, which predisposes patients to Salmonella infections, especially in bones. Salmonella tends to cause osteomyelitis, particularly in patients with sickle cell anemia

Other options:
A) Streptococcus can cause osteomyelitis, particularly in neonates or immunocompromised patients, it is not the most common organism associated with osteomyelitis in children with sickle cell disease
B) Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of osteomyelitis in general populations, but it is not typically the most common organism in children with sickle cell disease. While it can still be a pathogen, Salmonella is more commonly implicated in these cases
D) E. coli can cause osteomyelitis, but it is not the most common pathogen in sickle cell disease. Salmonella is far more frequent in these patients

q: A patient presented with jaundice, elevated bilirubin, and peripheral smear is as shown in the image. which of the following is associated with this condition?
e:
A. Mechanical 2nd heart sound
Explanation
Hemolytic anemia is often associated with prosthetic heart valves or other cardiac devices that can cause shear stress on red blood cells, leading to fragmentation (schistocytes). Patients with prosthetic valves may also have characteristic mechanical second heart sounds due to the artificial valve

Other options:
B) Heme in stools may indicate gastrointestinal bleeding, it is not a primary feature of mechanical hemolysis. This symptom is more relevant in conditions like gastrointestinal bleeding or malignancies
C) Splenomegaly is typically seen in hemolytic anemias caused by increased red blood cell destruction in the spleen (e.g., hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune hemolytic anemia), not in mechanical hemolytic anemia caused by shear stress
D) Goitre is associated with thyroid disorders, not mechanical hemolysis. It has no relevance to the condition described

q: A 27-year-old male presents with dyspnoea, unconscious 2 days after a road traffic accident. Likely diagnosis?
e:
A. Fat embolism
Explanation
Fat embolism syndrome is a common complication following fractures of long bones (e.g., femur) or pelvic trauma, often seen in young patients after road traffic accidents. It typically presents 24–72 hours after the injury with a triad of symptoms: respiratory distress (dyspnoea), neurological symptoms (unconsciousness, confusion), and a petechial rash (may not always be present). The timeline and presentation fit this diagnosis

Other options:
B) Thromboembolism: Thromboembolic events, such as a pulmonary embolism, are less likely in this case because the symptoms occurred 2 days post-accident and there is no evidence of deep vein thrombosis or hypercoagulability, which are common precursors
C) Air embolism typically occurs in specific scenarios, such as during surgery, central line placement, or penetrating chest trauma. This condition presents acutely, often immediately after the event, not delayed by 2 days
D) Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) is a condition characterized by widespread clotting and bleeding, often secondary to sepsis, trauma, or obstetric complications. While trauma can lead to DIC, the clinical presentation of dyspnoea and unconsciousness without bleeding or clotting symptoms makes DIC less likely

q: Which of the following are methods to delay aging process?
e:
C. Calorie restriction by 30%
Explanation
